68955cf5-ffa3-41df-b288-84241bf76ff4: Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Presented by Fort Mason Art Points Of Departure is a new series of immersive live events celebrating the spectrum of Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture (FMCAC) as a place for innovation and discovery, a personal port of embarkation for its community, and a window on the world. Each program celebrates the vibrant past, present, and future of FMCAC as it charts a course toward its 50th anniversary in 2027. Points Of Departure is curated by Brad Rosenstein, Associate Curator of Public Programs. Two Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Events Happen in The Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor Program 2 CIRCUS BY THE BAY Panel conversation and live performances Tuesday, October 13, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Cowell Theater, Pier 2/Gateway Pavilion, FMCAC , RESERVE SPACE Pickle Family Circus at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture Lively Arts Festival 1978. Photo: Terry Lorant In the 1970s, San Francisco became an epicenter of the emerging new American circus – an intimate one-ring model that spurned animal acts and focused on traditional skills of juggling, clowning, acrobatics, and aerial work, all filtered through a countercultural vaudevillian sensibility. This “not-so-big-top” was pioneered by such local companies as the Pickle Family Circus and its later incarnation, the New Pickle Circus, which performed annually at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture, and longtime FMCAC residents Make*A*Circus. This movement spawned a stream of Bay Area talents that spread their influence from Cirque du Soleil and Broadway to movies, and TV, an impact which resonates to this day. Join us for a magical evening celebrating this uniquely San Francisco history through a conversation with some of its leading lights, all veterans of Pickle Family Circus and the New Pickle Circus: performer/writer/director Gypsy Snider , trapeze artist/choreographer/director Shana Carroll , clown/writer/teacher Jeff Raz , and artistic director/choreographer Tandy Beal . The program includes rare archival photos and video, and live performances by Unique Derique ( Prescott Circus ), Chloe Somers Walier ( Dear San Francisco ), Elise Hing ( Circus Bella ), and performers from San Francisco Youth Circus ( SFYC ), Circus Center ’s pre-professional youth program. SFYC is led by Performance Coach Dominic Cruz , a 7 Fingers/ Dear San Francisco alum. (performers subject to change). Program 3 LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION Panel conversation and rare performance video Thursday, November 12, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center or Arts & Culture , RESERVE SPACE LEFT TO RIGHT: LIFE ON THE WATER’s Bill Talen , Ellen Sebastian , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert with a model of the Bayfront Theatre remodel 1987. LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW) was an extraordinary presenting and producing organization based at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture for seven seasons between 1986-1993. Centered in its own custom-designed space (now the Bayfront Theatre), the company was dedicated to presenting artists who originated their own work and committed to a blend of experimental and traditional stage forms, political statement, and cultural diversity. It became nationally renowned for its pioneering showcases of solo theater work by such luminaries as Spalding Gray and Karen Finley as well as co-producing the annual Solo Mio Festival. LOTW’s presentations also ranged from music, dance, screenings, and workshops to ongoing programs such as Latino Theatre Project, Earth Drama Lab, and AsianImprov aRts (AIR). This special evening reunites LOTW’s founding directors Ellen Sebastian Chang , Bill Talen , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert on their former stage for a sparkling conversation about the company’s groundbreaking work, which includes their own creations ranging from Pitt’s “avant mime” theater Not for Real and Sebastian’s epic The Sanctified Church to Talen’s biting satires such as Political Wife . The program includes never-before-seen archival video of some of LOTW’s most celebrated productions. Past Programs Program 1 TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Film screening and panel conversation Thursday, September 24, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture (FMCAC) , RESERVE SPACE TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Artist Alicia McCarthy Tell Them We Were Here (2021), a film by Griff Williams and Keelan Williams , chronicles visual/multidisciplinary artists currently living and working in the San Francisco Bay Area and how they extend the historical legacy of Bay Area creativity, activism, and community. Reflecting the spirit of FMCAC and its vibrant connection to local art and artists, the film centers the idea of art as a reflection of the place from which it emerges and helps to define the unique character of the Bay Area scene over the past 25 years. The film follows the work of Sadie Barnette , Amy Franceschini ( Futurefarmers ), Jim Goldberg , Tucker Nichols , Lynn Hershman Leeson , Alicia McCarthy , Nigel Poor ( Ear Hustle ), and M ichael Swaine , a select group of artists who have chosen a less-worn path. It touches on the disappearance of cultural communities due to gentrification and economic instability, while reminding us of art’s power to transform and how vital creative communities are to healthy societies and political change. The screening is followed by a panel discussion with director Griff Williams , artists Amy Franceschini and Tucker Nichols , and curator René de Guzman (all featured in the film), exploring how the local art scene has continued to evolve in the five years since the film’s premiere. All Fort Mason Art programs are generously supported by San Francisco Grants for The Arts, the FMCAC Board of Directors, and individual contributions to the Fort Mason Fund. PANELISTS & PERFORMERS PANELISTS TELL THEM WE WERE HERE : Griff Williams is an American painter, publisher and gallerist. In 1993 he founded Gallery 16 and the pioneering fine art printmaking workshop Urban Digital Color in San Francisco. The exhibition and publishing program has worked with hundreds of artists including Lynn Hershman Leeson, William Kentridge, Deborah Oropallo, Jim Isermann, bell hooks, Rex Ray, Margaret Kilgallen, Mark Grotjahn, Paul Sietsema, Arturo Herrera, Michelle Grabner, and Ari Marcopoulos. Williams has also designed and published dozens of acclaimed books with the Gallery 16 Editions imprint. His paintings have been exhibited in galleries and museums including the San Diego Museum of Art, the Crocker Art Museum in Sacramento, and the San Jose Museum of Art . His work has been reviewed in Art in America , Flash Art , and ARTnews . He co-directed Tell Them We Were Here with his son, Keelan Williams , a filmmaker based in Los Angeles. René de Guzman is a longtime Bay Area curator, artist, and arts consultant. He was one of the founding curators at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts as Visual Arts Curator and Director of Visual Arts, serving from 1993-2007, and subsequently served as the Senior Curator of Art and Director of Exhibition Strategy at the Oakland Museum of California from 2007-21. He also served as Deputy Director for Programs and Engagement at Headlands Center for the Arts , overseeing artist residencies and public programs. For more than three decades, he has developed innovative and popular exhibitions for a wide public and is currently Co-Director of Art + Water in San Francisco. Amy Franceschini is an artist whose work facilitates encounter, exchange, and tactile forms of inquiry by calling into question the “certainties” of a given time or place where a work is situated. In 1995, Franceschini founded Futurefarmers as a collaborative platform to consider the social, political, and environmental organization of space. Futurefarmers use various media to deconstruct systems to visualize and understand their intrinsic logics; food systems, public transportation, education … Through this disassembly they find new narratives and reconfigurations that form alternatives to the principles that once dominated these systems. Franceschini received her BFA in Photography from San Francisco State University and an MFA from Stanford University. She has taught in the visual arts graduate programs at California College of the Arts in San Francisco and Stanford University and in the Master of Eco-Social Design at the Free University in Bolzano, Italy. She is a 2009 Guggenheim Fellow, a 2019 Rome Prize Fellow and a 2017 recipient of the Herb Alpert Award for Visual Arts. Tucker Nichols is an artist based in Northern California. His work has been featured at the Drawing Center in New York, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Denver Art Museum, Den Frie Museum in Copenhagen, and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. A show of his sculpture, Almost Everything On The Table , was recently on view at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum. His drawings have been published in McSweeney’s , The Thing Quarterly , The New Yorker , and the Op-Ed pages of The New York Times . He is co-author of the books, Crabtree (with Jon Nichols) and This Bridge Will Not Be Gray (with Dave Eggers). Flowers for Sick People , his ongoing multimedia project, was featured on the PBS Newshour and the subject of an exhibition at SFMOMA, Close to Home: Creativity in Crisis , is an exhibition highlighting seven local artists’ responses to the pandemic. He is represented by ZieherSmith in New York and Gallery 16 in San Francisco. CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Gypsy Snider is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , now celebrating its fifth anniversary at the city’s historic Club Fugazi. As co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers , she wrote and directed SisterS , Réversible, Intersection , Amuse , Un D i a , Traces , and Loft . She has choreographed televised feature performances for America’s Got Talent and Her Majesty’s Royal Variety Performance . In 2013, working with director Diane Paulus on a new vision of Pippin , she created choreography and wove circus into the revival of the Broadway musical, earning her a Drama Desk Award and an Outer Critics Circle Award. Snider began her circus career at the age of four when her parents founded The Pickle Family Circus. She grew up touring the West Coast with the company. In 2002, while in her hometown of San Francisco, she wrote and directed for The New Pickle Circus a show entitled Circumstance , which premiered at FMCAC’s Cowell Theater. Snider is also a guest teacher and guest director at the National Circus School of Montreal. Shana Carroll is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , and co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers . Since the latter’s inception in 2002, Shana has directed, written, and created choreography for a dozen or so of their touring and/or resident shows, including Passagers , Cuisine & Confessions , Séquence 8 , and Traces . in 2024 Carroll was co-choreographer and Circus Designer for Water For Elephants on Broadway, for which she received the Chita Rivera Award for Best Choreography, as well as Tony, Drama Desk, and Outer Critics Circles nominations in the same category. Carroll has frequently collaborated with Cirque du Soleil , most recently as co-director of their first show on ice, Crystal , and previously as acrobatic designer and choreographer of Paramour (Broadway) and Iris (Los Angeles), and as director/choreographer of their performance at the 2012 Academy Awards. Originally from Berkeley, CA, and daughter of beloved San Francisco columnist Jon Carroll, Shana began her career as a trapeze artist with San Francisco’s Pickle Family Circus and went on to a 20-year career in the air with Cirque du Soleil and many others before co-founding The 7 Fingers. Jeff Raz has performed nationally and internationally for decades, starring in the Pickle Family Circus, Cirque du Soleil’s Corteo , Make*A*Circus, and many other circuses and theaters. Jeff is also a playwright, director, teacher, producer and has authored four books inspired by his career. Over the years he has also co-founded six arts organizations and worked globally as a communications and leadership consultant. Tandy Beal is a performer, director, choreographer, writer, teacher, and … dreamer. An off-the-map career includes: directing Pickle Family Circus for 10 years; touring four continents with Tandy Beal & Co.; writing/directing VIVA for the Moscow Circus in Japan; a show for NASA’s SETI project with Carl Sagan; projects with Lou Harrison, Frank Zappa, John Adams, and decades of projects with Bobby McFerrin, Art Lande, and Jon Scoville; choreographing opera, MTV, ballet; corporate shows (LucasFilms, SF 49ers, MCI, Coca-Cola, Pixar, Oracle+); acting off-Broadway; dancing for the Shah of Iran with Alwin Nikolais in Tehran; guest performances with Atlanta Ballet, Momix, Remy Charlip and in Europe, with Carolyn Carlson; creating what Dance Magazine said was the first contemporary dance/circus Nutcracker . Her life and work are featured in two books, The Pickle Clowns and Living Happily Ever After . She has received awards from AFI, CAC, NEA, Packard, and Hewlett +. Her natural habitat is the Santa Cruz mountains where she lives with longtime co-conspirator, Jon Scoville. PANELISTS LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION : Ellen Sebastian Chang is a distinguished multidisciplinary director, dramaturge, writer, and arts educator with a career spanning 50 years, dedicated to advocating for human rights and understanding through the creative arts. She has collaborated with a diverse array of artists and art forms: theater, opera, dance, radio, film and installation. Sebastian Chang commenced her career as a lighting technician and designer before making her debut as a director and writer in 1982 with Your Place Is No Longer With Us , an immersive play staged in private homes about a biracial girl. She co-founded LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW), a notable producing organization in San Francisco, and served as its co-artistic director. During her time at LOTW she created The Sanctified Church with Luisah Teisch, later renamed Sanctified with Esther Scott, No Trace of the Blonde with Holly Hughes, and Janie Geiser, FACE with Bob Ernst, Artis Fountaine, NAO, and Debora Iyall. She has been the creative director and teaching artist for The World As It Could Be Human Rights Education Program, utilizing the arts to deepen understanding of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and inspire activism across generations. Beyond her work in theater, she co-owned the award-winning FuseBOX restaurant in West Oakland created with Chef Sunhui Chang. She has received numerous grants and fellowships from prestigious arts foundations such as Creative Capital, Kenneth Rainin Foundation, MAP Fund, National Endowment for the Arts, and Ruth Arts Fellowship. Her current focus is rewilding six acres of land in the Pacific Northwest planting 1,350 native trees with foresters Boots on the Ground. William Talen grew up in small towns throughout Minnesota, South Dakota, and Wisconsin, and came west in the 70s, joining the poetry community in Bolinas, CA before moving to North Beach. Exploring storytelling techniques with solo shows in the Eureka Theater and Intersection, he studied with Spalding Gray and Sidney Lanier. Talen then partnered with Ellen Sebastian, and in 1984 they dreamed of a radical kind of theater, inspired by the stage sets of restaurants and the parties of Anon Salon, eventually lifting “Life on the Water” from a billboard in front of a yuppie apartment complex in Richmond, CA. Gathering with Joe Lambert and Leonard Pitt, LOTW kicked off with six weeks of Gray in the fall of ’86. After seven years, Talen departed for New York, leaving the Solo Mio Festival to Marcia Crosby, Joegh Bullock, and Kate Boyd. In New York and Europe, his character “Reverend Billy” caught a wave of post-religious spiritual hunger, inventing the movement against Consumerism by the time of 9/11. With director and life partner Savitri D, daughter Lena Nightstar, and a revolving troupe of 30 singers, the “Church of Stop Shopping” staged earth services at a series of NYC “art churches” and toured shows on five continents, always returning to justice campaigns in New York. In 2016, Neil Young and Daryl Hannah proposed that Talen preach his “Earthalujah” gospel at the opening of each show, which kicked off a 10-year collaboration, performing in 35 amphitheaters and reaching about 650,000 in Young’s rock audiences. Currently, the Stop Shopping Church has settled in the 500-seat Quaker Meetinghouse in Manhattan, the anti-consumerism of its early days now centered on the Earth’s crisis. Talen’s books include The Earth Wants You from City Lights, and now his fifth book, Earthalujah! , being published in November by Autonomedia Press. Leonard Pitt studied mime in Paris with Etienne Decroux for four years, becoming his assistant and performing in his company. On his return to the U.S., Pitt settled in Berkeley, CA, where he opened a school of physical theater, attracting students from around the world. Pitt’s one-man shows have received critical acclaim. He has performed and taught at theaters and festivals throughout the U.S., Europe, Brazil, New Zealand, and Australia. He was also a member of George Coates Performance Works and traveled widely with the company. In Bali he studied mask theatre and performed extensively with his teacher. In 1986, he co-founded LOTW, where his projects included the “avant-mime” production Not for Real (created with Rinde Eckert), Spleenix , The Art of Face , and performing David Barth’s solo play, Ned . In 1991, Leonard created Eco-Rap, an environmental education program combining ecology and rap music as a way to educate inner city youth about urgent social issues. He has written and published seven books, including three books on Paris and a memoir, and created numerous videos on Paris, all viewable on YouTube ( Leonard Pitt Paris ). He continues to live in Berkeley and create and is currently working on two new books. Joe Lambert is the founder of StoryCenter and the originator of the digital storytelling movement, a participatory media methodology used by 100,000s of people all over the world. The work has taken him and his organization to all 50 U.S. states, and more than 90 countries. Earlier in his career, he served as Executive Director of the People’s Theater Coalition and LOTW, where he executive-produced more than 500 performances, festivals, conferences, and national gatherings. Highlights include the first San Francisco Jazz Tap Festival, collaborations with artists like Guillermo Gomez Peña, the Blue Man Group, Marty Pottenger, and Dana Atchley. During that time, he held leadership roles in national initiatives including the Alliance for Cultural Democracy and the National Performance Network, and served as a panelist and principal consultant for numerous public agencies and private foundations. As an author and curriculum developer, he has written numerous articles. For projToday, based in Santa Fe, NM, he continues this work through StoryHost LLC, teaching workshops, hosting the Elderware podcast, and exploring the intersections of story, aging, and meaning-making. PERFORMERS CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Unique Derique , an internationally acclaimed entertainer, is a cornerstone of the Bay Area circus and performing arts scene. He honed his physical comedy with premier troupes including Circus A La Mode, Make*A*Circus, and the historic Pickle Family Circus. Dedicated to community arts education, Derique has spent nearly three decades as an Artist-in Residence at West Oakland’s Prescott Circus Theater, teaching youth the art and history of Hambone body percussion. His versatile talent has graced international television and stages worldwide, opening for legends like Lou Rawls, Sammy Davis Jr., and The Temptations. Annually, his holiday show Fool La La: Whimsical brings joy to all ages at The Marsh Berkeley. Elise Hing , born and raised in Santa Cruz, CA, discovered her natural flexibility at age 12 and quickly developed a passion for contortion. For the past five years she has performed with Circus Bella doing free shows in the park during the summer and under the big top in the winter for their holiday spectacular. She has also appeared with Flynn Creek Circus and continues to gig all over the bay area. Hing loves to connect and delight audiences through her playful, awe-inspiring shapes and movements but outside of the ring she enjoys being out in nature with friends and pursuing creative projects like sewing. Chloe Somers Walier , known as the “Megawatt Smile,” is an effervescent circus performer with eight years of international touring experience with Les 7 Doigts de la main, performing in Passengers , Duel Reality , and Dear San Francisco . A multidisciplinary performer specializing in hula hoop, trapeze, group acrobatics, and bottle walking – balancing in heels on top of wine bottles – she has performed at three international circus festivals and received the People’s Choice Award from Riga Cirks. With a love for the unexpected and a playful spirit at the heart of her work, she brings a warm, joyful energy to the stage, blending technical skill and theatricality with a little bit of sparkle and a lot of personality. Set against the charged intimacy of a Southern college town, Danny O’Dea’s debut follows Michael McKnight, a young man orbiting grief, desire, and moral uncertainty as he navigates friendship, sexuality, faith, and the quiet violence of complicity. With prose that is sharp, intimate, and darkly funny, O’Dea captures the intoxicating freedom of youth alongside its moral blind spots, asking how responsibility is formed, deferred, or abandoned altogether. Choose the conversation or decision that can no longer be avoided. Define one capability or practical experiment to begin now. Managers and team leads navigating AI adoption, restructuring, new systems, changing priorities, or pressure to move faster. People and organizational leaders responsible for supporting teams through role change. What you leave with A clear map of the change you are navigating. One conversation or decision to move forward. Measles, an explosive cyclospora outbreak, a hantavirus scare aboard a cruise ship, an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, rising sexually transmitted infections, and an HIV pandemic playing out amid U.S. funding cuts to global health. Meanwhile, COVID-19 is never fully out of the picture. 6e1a5914-62f6-44bd-9ab0-57407fafff76: The revolution had a sex life. · The late 1960s told young women to get free—sexually, politically, artistically. And for many, those freedoms were exhilarating. But liberation could also create contradictions of its own. In Alexis Krasilovsky’s new novel, Portrait of an Artist as a Young Woman , an aspiring filmmaker plunges into the art and sexual experimentation of the era, navigating desire, ambition, creative possibility, exploitation, and old hierarchies in new clothes. Judy Juanita’s Virgin Soul , meanwhile, follows a young Black woman drawn into the revolutionary politics of the Black Panther Party, where idealism, danger, race, sex, and power collide. Krasilovsky and Juanita—whose own lives intersect with the histories their novels revisit—come together at Clio’s to interrogate the mythology of liberation from the inside. What did “free love” offer women, and what did it demand of them? Could radical movements escape the inequalities of the society they wanted to overthrow? And what did it take for a woman to insist on being not someone’s muse, girlfriend, comrade, or supporting character, but an artist and political actor in her own right? Moving between fiction and lived history, from the New York art world and the emergence of women filmmakers to the Black Panthers and Oakland, their conversation asks what happens when women tell the story of a supposedly liberated generation for themselves. Alexis Krasilovsky is an award-winning filmmaker, author, and Professor Emerita of Cinema and Television Arts at California State University, Northridge. A member of Yale’s first coeducational graduating class, she made End of the Art World , featuring Andy Warhol, Robert Rauschenberg, Jasper Johns, Roy Lichtenstein, and other major artists. Her decades-long work on women and filmmaking includes the documentary Women Behind the Camera and the books Women Behind the Camera: Conversations with Camerawomen and Shooting Women: Behind the Camera, Around the World . Her new novel, Portrait of an Artist as a Young Woman , will be published by City Point Press in September 2026. Judy Juanita is an award-winning poet, novelist, playwright, and essayist whose work spans race, gender, radical politics, and California life. Her semi-autobiographical novel Virgin Soul follows a young Black woman drawn into the Black Panther Party in the late 1960s. Her recent books include the memoir California Fever Dream and Abortion (or Woman as Threefold Murderess) . Her poetry collection Manhattan my ass, you’re in Oakland won the 2021 American Book Award from the Before Columbus Foundation, and her essay collection DeFacto Feminism: Essays Straight Outta Oakland examines race, gender, politics, and spirituality through the perspective of a Black activist and self-described “feminist foot soldier.”

f3e3362e-2294-457a-92ab-1c865c45024a: Sitting at the forefront of contemporary jazz · 'Well, at least nobody could ever accuse us of releasing too much music!’ quips GregCarmichael on the release of their latest EP “The Empire of Lights”, ‘but I think our fans know by now that we’re a little obsessive about only releasing music when we have something ready that we really love.’ The four tracks on their latest release visit familiar themes for longtime fans, from the western shuffle of “8,000 Miles” to the reggae flavours of “Alisio”, the upbeat joy of “Back to Back” to the laid back groove of “Other People”. ‘We hope there’s something here for everyone,” says Miles Gilderdale, “we’re very lucky that over the years we’ve found fans that just get what we’re doing, so we can wear our influences on our sleeves and not have to try and fit into any one style.’ With over 35 years of recording and touring, the band’s longevity may be due in part to that spirit of never trying to fit in, but to just making music that they love. ‘I feel really grateful that we’ve been on such a long journey with our fans and they’re still there with us.’ Greg says, ‘We talk after shows, and it’s always such an honor to hear the stories of how our music has been the soundtrack to so many people’s lives.’ This EP is the first of a series of shorter musical releases that will eventually combine into a full album.’ Miles says, ‘We know that these days people listen to our music in lots of different ways, but I think we all remember the thrill of bringing a new record home and listening from start to finish, so we try and make sure everything we release works in that way as well as on playlists.’ The Empire of Lights will be released to all music platforms worldwide on June 13th, 2025, and a limited run of CDs will be pressed to be available to purchase at live shows.

202272e5-008b-46ec-9357-a64d84e01da3: Patrick Wolff is a saxophone and clarinet player with a long history in the jazz scenes of New York City and San Francisco. He has performed or recorded with Albert "Tootie" Heath, Matt Wilson, Grant Stewart, Louis Moholo-Moholo, Dena Derose, and many other jazz greats. Since moving to San Francisco in 2009, Wolff has played and recorded regularly in the bands of Marcus Shelby, Richard Sears, Graham Connah, Adam Shulman, and Diana Gameros. Outside of the jazz world, he has had an eclectic mix of work including long stints in West African pop/funk group Asiko, prog metal band Kayo Dot, and with fuji music legend Adewale Ayuba. With six albums released under his name, Wolff has made his mark as a bandleader with various groups playing his original compositions, and with classic jazz quartets and quintets focused on repertoire of the bebop and hard bop eras. His playing is characterized by a focus on lyricism and an embrace of the whole lineage of jazz styles. Wolff is also a passionate jazz educator and advocate. For four years, he hosted and produced a weekly fearure show on KCSM 91.1FM ("Have You Heard"), exploring the work of emerging and underrated jazz artists, and continues to dj for the station on occasion. He was the Faculty Director at the Stanford Jazz Workshop from 2008-2013, and currently teaches jazz history, composition, and ensemble classes at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music and the College of San Mateo throughout the year, and at the Stanford Jazz Workshop in the summer.

97ba1252-ed02-4de5-ad6c-d5e71d62fadb: Gothic and atmospheric, Raven is an aching tale of loss, freedom, death, and resurrection by the celebrated author of Jane Steele and Dust and Shadow . “A clever, darkly funny, and enthralling tale that keeps us turning the pages, even as it explores themes of love and loss, deception, death, and resurrection. Here Faye has performed alchemy, turning the words on the page into gothic gold.” — Lisa Unger An orphaned young woman in antebellum Maryland is pulled into a maelstrom of passion, pain, and occult power in this Gothic homage to the life and works of Edgar Allan Poe. Raven Helen Alan has always been haunted by witchcraft. Since the death of her beloved mother, she has soothed herself by speaking words into spells—a proclivity enhanced by time spent with her aunt’s library of occult books. After an itinerant childhood, Raven is relieved to finally settle down with Aunt Berenice in her Baltimore townhouse. There she finds a long-sought sense of belonging with the family of enslaved workers in her aunt’s household, especially the brilliantly odd youngest daughter Pym. Raven’s infatuation with her friend only grows more intimate as the girls become women together. But when the household is threatened with financial ruin, Raven must set out to earn her own living. Taking a job as a paid companion, Raven arrives at the crumbling Moldavia Manor. Her charge is a delicate young invalid named Lenore Legrand who haunts the Gothic structure like a phantom. Living with them is Lenore’s devoted older cousin Travanion, who spends his days searching ancient texts for an Elixir of Life that might cure Lenore. Raven finds herself inexorably drawn to both cousins as well as the to secrets hidden in the shadows of Moldavia Manor. But those secrets may just be the death of her... “A literary high wire act—combining clever homage with creativity and passion, a celebration of all things Poe, and treasures galore for fans to discover. Raven is the new essential gothic—layered, compelling, witty and entirely entertaining.” —Hank Phillippi Ryan Lyndsay Faye is the internationally bestselling author of eight critically acclaimed novels and two short story collections. She has been published in fifteen languages, nominated for two Edgar Awards, and received an American Library Association award for Best Historical Novel. A notable writer of Sherlock Holmes pastiches including Dust and Shadow and Observations by Gaslight , she also particularly enjoys upending classical literature, as in Jane Steele , which transforms Jane Eyre into a feminist serial killer. A true New Yorker in the sense that she was born elsewhere, Faye lives in Queens with her husband Nicholas and her cat Prufrock. f504f699-769e-46d0-ae85-ab9bbc6dcbd6: How Trees Make Our World · Robert Macfarlane writes “There is no lone tree language, but a forest of tree languages.” In The Language of Trees , Katie Holten invites us to enter some of these forests. She created a Tree Alphabet to translate a compendium of well known, loved, lost and new writing. She takes readers on a journey from creation myths and cave paintings to the death of a 3,500 year-old cypress tree, from Tree Clocks in Mongolia and forest fragments in the Amazon to Emerson’s language of fossil poetry, unearthing a grove of beautiful stories along the way. Listening, speaking, reading and writing are how humans communicate and make sense of the world. The alphabet is how we organize information and knowledge; our networked world depends on it. Trees, the font, lets us renew our relationships with language, landscape, perception, time, memory and reading itself by slowing the reader down to decipher words in the woods. Katie Holten will be in conversation with writer and editor Marthine Satris to discuss our relationship with literature and landscape and the unexpected and imaginative language inspired by the beauty of the natural world. Katie Holten is an award-winning artist and environmental activist. Holten's work investigates the entangled relationships between humans and the natural world. At the root of her practice is a call for Rights of Nature and a commitment to fighting the climate and biodiversity emergency. Her collaborative research based work explores the inextricable relationship between organic systems and human-made systems. She has created Tree Alphabets , a Forest Alphabet , and a Wildflower Alphabet to share the joy she finds in her love of the more-than-human world. Her work has appeared in The New Yorker, The New York Times, Artforum, and The Guardian. She is a visiting lecturer at the New School of the Anthropocene. Katie Holten’s book The Language of Trees was published in 2023 and became an instant bestseller. Holten lives between New York City and Ireland. If she could be a tree, she would be an Oak. Marthine Satris is a writer and editor living in Oakland. She is the Associate Publisher at Heyday, the nonprofit press in Berkeley, where she edits books about California's history, culture, and natural world. Her own poetry and prose have been published in The Georgia Review, The San Francisco Chronicle, Antiphony Journal, Santa Clara Review, Ballast Journal , and elsewhere. She is a frequent contributor to Oakland Review of Books.

dc341efb-c1b8-5e60-99a4-292e63e4faf9: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

3fd127df-75d1-4215-928f-3ac41b5e71d0: The best-selling author of "Fed Up" shares her brave and intimate memoir which shows how women's anger can lead us towards change. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Wednesday, October 14 when best-selling author Gemma Hartley comes to the store to share her new memoir No One Loves an Angry Woman: An Exvangelical Coming-of-Rage Story. Gemma will be joined in conversation by Tracy Clark-Flory and will sign copies of her book after the presentation. “A seething read that burns to the bone.” —Tia Levings, New York Times best-selling author of A Well-Trained Wife Gemma Hartley grew up in an Evangelical household where she was raised to become an obedient wife from the time she was a little girl. A sexual assault as a teenager upended her evangelical world, and that coupled with an upbringing steeped in purity culture led her to internalize guilt, silence… and anger. The good girl conditioning of the church demanded that Hartley seek the narrow path of womanhood that emphasized service to others, to swallow the discomfort and rage that simmered just below the surface – but when political events reawakened her trauma, she began to come apart at the seams. Here she unravels the threads of her upbringing to weave a new story, one where women’s anger is not sinful and dangerous – it is information, and often the most rational response there is. Whether or not you’ve ever set foot in a church, Christian patriarchal norms have shaped American culture in ways that are far-reaching and insidious. From restrictive legislation that takes away women’s bodily autonomy to cultural norms that expect women to pick up after their husbands and joyfully give up their careers to care for children—these are all standards informed and fed by Christian culture. Tying together her Christian upbringing together with a feminist examination of society today, Hartley tells her personal story, but it’s bigger than that: No One Loves an Angry Woman is the story of a cultural awakening.

Dinosaurs were the dominant large animals on Earth for well over 100 million years, and they still manage to captivate generation after generation of humans. b379d588-3736-4c6b-9f31-f39aa6c0ad21: Formed in 2019, Anhad Naad Collective is a genre-defying ensemble rooted in the exploration of South Asian musical traditions and their intersections with global genres. The collective had its debut concert in 2020 in San Francisco, led by core members Divya Purohit Vyas and Jun Ishimuro (of Qb Moda Jazz). Initially, their work centered around blending South Asian raga-based music with the soulful textures of jazz, R&B, and Black musical traditions. With a flexible and evolving lineup of collaborating artists, Anhad Naad Collective has performed at notable Bay Area venues including Bird & Beckett, Integral Yoga Institute, the Golden Gate Park Bandstand, and events such as San Francisco’s Summer of Music hosted by Noise Pop. In 2023, the group expanded its focus to delve deeper into South Asian spiritual music, with a special emphasis on Sufi Qawwali traditions. Anhad Naad treats the spiritual dimension of Sufi poetry and music with deep reverence, often seeking guidance from poets and experts from Pakistan and India. Lead vocalist Divya Purohit Vyas has previously been a part of Bay Dervish in Alameda, a spiritual music collective associated with Sufi Way, led by the late Kiran Rana and Jeanne Rana. Anhad Naad Collective Current Members: • Divya Purohit Vyas – Vocals • Irum Aftab – Vocals • Vivek Anand – Vocals, Harmonium • Rajnish Kamat – Vocals • Jun Ishimuro – Flute, Digital Audio Workstation (DAW)

That storied history includes the 1967 founding of Rolling Stone. As both Peter Richardson and Charles Ponce de Leon relate in recent books, for a decade (before decamping for NYC), the magazine was at the vanguard of West Coast counterculture, launching dozens of journalists’ careers and setting new standards for writing about music and culture. Where better, then, to reunite folks with first-hand knowledge of those SF roots, including Ben Fong-Torres and Marianne Partridge, than at the new Counterculture Museum? The result is a “multi-dimensional rock” identity that has continuously evolved over the past decade, as the band members themselves – Ben Stevens (vocals, keys), Christian Rose (vocals, violin), Kamau Burton (vocals, guitar), Daniel Moss (guitar), and Rami El-Abidin (bass) – went from students at Boston College to professional touring musicians and seasoned recording artists. Juice’s sound may be ever-evolving, but their bold energy is evergreen: The goal, both on stage and on record, is not just to connect on a human level, but to breathe life into every room. While they pack a punch on record, Juice shine their brightest onstage, bringing their music to life for all to see, hear, and feel. The band have played countless national tours over the past ten years, including four headline tours and support slots opening for bands like flipturn, Ocean Alley, and The Dip.

I realised I had to get my shit together here.” As if the matter was ever in doubt, hours later, he did just that. The stranger’s assertion that anyone stepping up to the microphone with the band who terrorised a nation faces one of the tallest orders in rock and roll – make no mistake, filling big shoes requires big cojones – overlooked the fact that he was speaking to one of the few singers, and perhaps even the < Such was its success, in fact, that this short series of concerts has blossomed into a busy diary. This year, Carter and the Pistols – drummer Paul Cook, guitarist Steve Jones and bassist Glen Matlock – are set to perform in Australia, New Zealand, Japan, the United States of America, mainland Europe, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere. They’ll headline halls and appear at festivals. In March, the group will top the bill at a Teenage Cancer Trust concert at the Royal Albert Hall, of all places. Much more of this and they’ll be playing at Buckingham Palace. For anyone who might be wondering, they’re doing these things because, in 2025, the Pistols are sensational once more. And they’re doing it is because they want to. “What I live by now is, if it ain’t fun, I ain’t doing it,” the always reliably blunt Steve Jones says. “I’m too fucking old to be putting up with a bunch of old shit and acting like everything’s cool just to keep the ball rolling. Those days are gone. If it ain’t fun, honestly, I’m out of here. I ain’t got the energy for any crap any more.” The credit for bringing Frank Carter into the orbit of the Pistols belongs to Glen Matlock’s youngest son. As a member of the erstwhile group Dead!, Louis Matlock had seen the singer leading the charge while touring the UK as special guests to Frank Carter & The Rattlesnakes. Night after night, he witnessed the fearlessness of a performer who approached live music as if it were a collision sport. Big shoes be damned, if you’re looking for a singer, the son told the father, Frank’s your man. “Louis said, the guy you need is Frank Carter,” Glen Matlock says. “So I got his number off him and we arranged to have a coffee. I didn’t know much about him but Louis was always going on about him. So we had a play with him and Paul – Steve was out of the country – and Paul liked him, as did I, so we told Steve. I also went to see the Rattlesnakes at the Roundhouse [in Camden Town], where they did two sold out nights, and I was impressed. Then Steve came over [from his home in Los Angeles] and we started rehearsing and that was it.” Asked to nominate the exact point at which he realised that this new version of the Sex Pistols became a force to be reckoned with, Paul Cook replies that it was during the marching-boots style drum intro to Holidays In The Sun, the first song on the first night at Bush Hall. “As soon as we did Holidays… I thought, ‘Yeah, this is working,” he says. “This is going to be brilliant. This is going to be fantastic.” I was at the back there, looking at Frank with his red hair, and I was kind of getting flashbacks a little bit. I just thought, ‘Wow, this is how it was and how it should be’.” Naturally, Carter himself needed no introduction to the Sex Pistols. Raised in a home in the satellite town of Watford that groaned from the weight of vinyl LPs, as a 14-year-old, he would listen to his father’s copy of the epochal Never Mind The Bollocks… Here’s The Sex Pistols whenever his parents were out of the house. Smitten by its irresistible mix of fury and wit, blood and thunder, like countless other artists-to-be before him, he was at once captivated. Its guiding light helped lead him to the stage, and, in time, to < “The one thing I took from the album that I put immediately into the way I perform was just the energy of it,” Carter says. “I’ve heard records that < So, please, let us not be in any doubt as to his credentials as an MC of chaos. In 2008, 36 years after two members of the Pistols challenged each other to a fight after discovering they were playing different songs onstage at the 100 Club, at the same venue, as the singer with Gallows, Carter chased an audience member who had thrown a pint of lager onstage up the venue’s stairs and out onto Oxford Street < He even helped orchestrate his own Great Rock and Roll Swindle. In 2009, after Warner Bros. signed Gallows for a million quid, the group handed their new label the pummelling and furious Grey Britain, an album that seemed designed to repel the casual listener. “Britain is fucked,” Carter said at the time. “Grey Britain is all about what’s going on socially, politically and economically in the UK, and how it affects us.” Sound familiar? As in, there is no future in England’s dreaming? Of course, in 2025, bands and artists are less inclined than they once were to sing about issues that affect and bedevil an entire nation. With social media replacing punk rock as the fastest route into the public bloodstream, rock and roll has entered an introspective phase. Just as well, then, that the Pistols’ State of the Union Address remains as pressing, and as prescient, as ever. Inevitably, in the (almost) half century that has elapsed since a pair of Millwall supporting hot dog vendors in Piccadilly Circus unwittingly provided Steve Jones with the title for his group’s sole bona fide album – “never mind the bollocks,” they would say, meaning “don’t bother with that…” – London and Britain have changed almost beyond recognition. But at street level, the problems and frustrations remain the same. The Pistols themselves, though, < It’s different, too, because in 2025 the group’s personnel no longer comprises elements of soap opera, or pantomime. Instead, unity and teamwork are the makings of the new machine; the cohesion of drums, bass, guitar and voice in the service of the songs. In this iteration, the rock and roll itself is allowed to shine, timeless and evergreen. There is no swindle. The people who wrote and played the music back in ’76 and ’77 are able to enjoy it anew. “Don’t forget, the three of us learned to play together,” Glen Matlock says. “It was all pretty much at a similar level of competency when we started out. And we kind of grew together as musicians.” And now? “Put it this way,” he adds, “someone who is close to the band, I won’t say who, said it’s the first time they’ve seen us coming offstage with smiles on our faces since ’96. Which is good, because life’s too short for all that bollocks, really.” As for what might come after the Sex Pistols have said hello and goodnight to audiences across the globe, no one is saying because no one seems to know. The promise of new music that was extinguished by a television interview with Bill Grundy and the subsequent shellshock of a young band receiving too much of everything, far too soon for anyone, may never be realised. But who can say for sure? At least for now, there’s no point in asking - you’ll get no reply. But what we do have, for sure, is Frank Carter and the Sex Pistols whipping up a storm across the globe in a manner that is familiar but fresh, old but new. Catch it while you can, for as long as it lasts. Because we won’t see their kind again.

3f5280fb-1759-531a-80f0-c18dd2626df4: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com

de03486a-6131-4f21-a150-f8b6139935b7: The 100 th anniversary of John Coltrane’s birthday has inspired dozens of performances across the Bay Area this year, but no artist is better equipped to evoke the legacy of the saxophone titan and spiritual seeker than Richard Howell . An acclaimed musician, composer and educator, he defines his performances as “Bridge Music,” a jazz pathway that creates sonic connection across obstacles and differences. It’s music that celebrates diversity as it bridges, unites and merges the experience of all listeners, an approach rooted in the spirit of John Coltrane’s “A Love Supreme.” Howell, who spent years on the road with Etta James, also embraces the contradiction of James Brown’s simple yet intricate African-inspired rhythmic concepts and the deep soulfulness of the Isley Brothers. As a saxophonist and vocalist, he has a gift for connecting to multi-generational audiences with an abiding spirituality that invites all listeners to partake. He’s particularly eager to present an afternoon honoring the spirit and music of John Coltrane, he explains. “I’ve had the blessing of a close relationship with his son, Ravi Coltrane, as my son Elé has been part of Ravi’s rhythm section as a drummer for the past seven years. What I’m envisioning is an acoustic jazz quartet – tenor saxophone, acoustic piano, bass and drums – rooted in the Coltrane tradition, but also reflecting the living continuum of that music.”

e4f11d3b-b9bb-48f2-9c26-b1a35ab5df08: The acclaimed author and illustrator share a new picture book written in haiku, offering a window into the world of snow monkeys in Japan. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Thursday, October 15 at 5:00 PM when acclaimed local author Maggie Tokuda-Hall and illustrator Yas Imamura come to the store to share their latest picture book, Bathtime for Snow Monkeys. Maggie and Yas will sign copies of their book after the presentation. At the Jigokudani monkey park in Nagano, nihonzaru—Japanese macaques—have a unique way of de-stressing from life in a cold climate: gathering in their very own onsen, or hot spring “spa,” to lounge and snack. Peek into this magical world in the mountains, hushed by snow, where the macaques reign over their onsen, huddling together. As a playful baby monkey splashes, the others don’t want to join in, and as the baby’s amusing antics wind down, parents and little ones reading the story will happily snuggle together like the macaques, warm and safe. Maggie Tokuda-Hall’s soothing narration, written entirely in haiku form—as befits its Japanese subject and natural themes—pairs with gorgeous illustrations by Yas Imamura. An author’s note offers insight into the habitat displacement and human intervention that led to the monkeys taking over this toasty, tranquil gathering spot. MAGGIE TOKUDA-HALL is the author of numerous award-winning, best-selling children's and young adult books including Love In the Library ; The Mermaid, The Witch, and the The Sea duology; Squad; and The Worst Ronin . She has been called "... one of the most unflinching voices in contemporary genre literature." Her writing has been featured in Harper's Bazaar, Electric Literature, Densho, and more. Maggie is also a founding member and national leader of Authors Against Book Bans. She lives in Oakland, California, with her husband, children, and objectively perfect dog YAS IMAMURA is an illustrator based in Portland, Oregon, working primarily in gouache and watercolor. She is best known for her work in children's publishing, including Love In the Library by Maggie Tokuda-Hall, The Very Oldest Pear Tree by Nancy I. Sanders, a Yoko Ono biography titled Can You Imagine? by Lisa Tolin, and more. Yas occasionally teaches as an adjunct faculty member at Pacific Northwest College of Art.
c7d987bb-3c76-4b77-982d-9aa28169272d: A somatic workshop to understand your nervous system, reconnect with your body, and learn practical tools for real transformation... Have you ever known exactly what you "should" do, but still found yourself stuck in the same patterns? Maybe you've read the books, listened to the podcasts, journaled, reflected, and tried to think your way into change. Yet anxiety, overwhelm, self-sabotage, emotional reactivity, procrastination, or feeling disconnected from yourself keep showing up. That's because lasting transformation doesn't happen through the mind alone. It happens through the body. In this immersive workshop, you'll learn the foundations of somatic healing and nervous system regulation, and why working with your body is often the missing piece when it comes to creating meaningful, sustainable change. We'll explore how stress, emotions, beliefs, and protective patterns are stored in the body, and why healing becomes more effective when we include the nervous system in the process. You'll learn: What somatics actually is (and why it's becoming more popular) Why mindset work alone isn't enough to create real, lasting change How your nervous system influences your emotions, behaviors, and daily experiences Simple somatic tools you can use to feel more grounded, present, and connected How to work with your body instead of constantly trying to push through or override it This workshop isn't just educational — you'll also experience somatics firsthand through guided practices, including breathwork, body awareness, grounding exercises, mindful movement, and embodiment practices designed to help you reconnect with yourself and your body's wisdom. The honesty and rigor of this book is a gift.” —Amanda Montei, author of Touched Out “Hartley’s tour de force will enliven, embolden, and wake you up.” —Kate Manne, author of Down Girl Gemma Hartley is the author of Fed Up: Emotional Labor, Women, and the Way Forward . cf65d47d-c967-489e-885a-eeef225ac2a6: Rainforest Radicals presents the first history of one of the most innovative and successful environmental organizations of the late twentieth century. Rainforest Action Network emerged in 1985, when it took over a fledgling effort to protect rainforests from transnational corporations funding the expansion of tropical cattle ranching. It excelled at using nonviolent, civil disobedience in dramatic campaigns that captured the attention of the public, media, and RAN’s corporate adversaries. As a result, two decades later rainforest conservation went from a niche academic topic to a fixture in American popular culture, the rights of Indigenous people had gone from ignored or romanticized to at least considered in discussions of the management of their ancestral homelands, and RAN had scored a series of victories over some of the planet’s largest corporations. In Rainforest Radicals David Benac traces the evolution of RAN and radical, transnational grassroots environmentalism through the four campaigns identified at the group’s founding: rainforest beef, Hawai‘ian rainforests, tropical timber, and multinational development banks. Forty years after RAN’s inception, there is much to learn from how it organized people in small towns and large cities across the United States, created alliances that spanned oceans, and inspired a new movement that integrated human rights, Indigenous sovereignty, and environmental protection to challenge multinational corporations, national governments, and neocolonial corporate-led globalism. Through more than thirty oral histories, including those of key players from different eras of RAN’s history as well as leaders from other environmental and Indigenous rights organizations, Rainforest Radical s provides unparalleled insight into the network. “This history of Rainforest Action Network is necessary for our times. From civil disobedience in Hawai‘i to raucous protests in the aisles of Home Depot and annual auto shows in the 1990s, the pages of Rainforest Radicals offer uplifting stories of solidarity and blueprints for successful (and not-so-successful) actions. I could easily see this being a sort of guidebook for grassroots activists today.”—Allyson P. Brantley, author of Brewing a Boycott: How a Grassroots Coalition Fought Coors and Remade American Consumer Activism David Benac is an associate professor of history and public history coordinator at Western Michigan University. He is the author of Conflict in the Ozarks: Hill Folk, Industrialists, and Government in the Courtois Hills . Ukraïne: Recipes and Stories from Kyiv to the Black Sea - Experience the joy and resilience of Ukrainian cuisine in this visually rich, travelogue-style cookbook filled with 100 traditional and modern recipes that highlight the comforting dishes, distinctive flavors, and time-honored techniques that make this food so extraordinary. Ukrainian chef Anna Voloshyna traveled across the diverse regions of her homeland―from the mountains to coastline, cities to grasslands, forests to wine country―collecting recipes, stories, and friendships to answer the question: What is Ukrainian cuisine? In these pages, she takes you along on this appetizing and fascinating journey. Vivid and poignant storytelling transports you to the boisterous streets of Kyiv where food carts sell aromatic sausages; to cool root cellars, a fixture in Ukrainian households, their walls stocked with jars of preserved and fermented deliciousness; and to the front line of the war where Voloshyna cooked a meal for fifty soldiers fighting for their country. Stunning photos bring you to the fields of sunflowers that blanket the steppe every summer; the shimmering waters of the Black Sea, brimming with marine life; and the imposing Carpathian peaks where flocks of sheep wander, their milk used to make beloved bryndza cheese. A treasure trove of recipes, drawn from all these places, bring a taste of Ukraine to your table, including: Beet and Plum Lemonade Cold Soup with Fresh and Fermented Tomatoes Grilled Sardines with Dilly Potatoes Mom’s Chicken and Potato Roast Lamb Plov with Apples and Chickpeas No-Churn Sunflower Seed Butter Ice Cream Plus, Sour Cucumbers, Beet Kvas, Mushroom Salt, Smoked Honey, and more pantry staples that will enhance your everyday cooking At a critical juncture in the nation's history, this cookbook seeks to preserve Ukraine's rich culinary heritage. By documenting recipes along with countless stories and images in a lustrous package, Ukraïne captures the very essence of the place while offering an acknowledgment of the country’s enduring spirit and a way to keep its culinary identity alive, preserving its past and ensuring its future.

a680133c-4709-4073-99d7-4b4c3dcd53e7: Our Loving Companions is a groundbreaking immersive theater experience celebrating the beautiful bond at the heart of pet ownership. A bond strong enough to propel us through deeply painful loss, time and again. Over 90 minutes, audiences journey through the laughter, devotion, inexplicable joy, and grief that define our relationships with our animal companions. Most shows will have a facilitated discussion afterwards for those who desire to partake. A portion of each $100 Companion Circle Ticket is donated to Bay Area animal charities to support animals in need. “The Bridge” by Jay Cross “What We Know” by Stephanie Weisman “A Dog Dreams” by Jeffrey Fisher Smith ”A Little Bird Told Me” by Marilyn Anderson “Must Love Pitbulls” by Jenny Mead “Tomorrow” by Alan Stewart “Outside the Box” by Emily Turner “A Good Dog” by Laura Neill “Ellie’s Goodbye” by Leslie Corn “Like a Dog”by Anya Martin “For The Love Of Buddy” by Dyanna Morrison “Roll Over, a monologue from the cat’s point of view” by Tommy Our Loving Companions is the result of a shared artistic vision between Grief Dialogues founder Elizabeth Coplan and co-producer and playwright Alan Stewart . Recognizing the need for an animal-centered immersive experience, Coplan envisioned a space that honors the distinct and deeply personal nature of the creatures who share our homes, our routines, and our unconditional love. Stewart, a producer, playwright, Dramatist Guild Foundation Fellow, and former trustee of San Francisco’s Magic Theatre, brings a distinctive artistic voice shaped by his first career as a veterinary internist and a lifelong belief in the human-animal bond as a language of the heart. Together, they create theater that invites audiences not only to witness grief, but to experience it in a way that clarifies, deepens, and transforms. As founder and Artistic Director of The Marsh, Stephanie Weisman brings a deep appreciation for work that blends storytelling with emotional truth, making her collaboration with Our Loving Companions a natural and meaningful fit. She is delighted to welcome Grief Dialogues to both The Marsh San Francisco and Berkeley—spaces long dedicated to bold, intimate, and transformative performance. Through hundreds of productions each year, alongside classes, youth programs, and live music, The Marsh has become a home for stories that matter. Stephanie’s own work in grief-centered theater, including her play 180 Days, To Die. To Live. , reflects that same commitment to exploring life’s most tender moments with honesty and care. And at home, her own loving companions—Marsh mascots Marsha and Junior—are never far from heart, a daily reminder of the deep bonds this experience so beautifully honors. Under the consulting direction of Dani Davis , Our Loving Companions living, immersive theatrical experience invites audiences to move through a curated landscape of short plays, poetry, music, sculpture, shared reflection, and personal stories. Blending warmth, tenderness, reverence, and moments of gentle humor, the production explores death, loss, and remembrance through what follows the final goodbye…the empty leash, the quiet food bowl, the space at the foot of the bed. Each performance is carefully choreographed behind the scenes to create an atmosphere fostering connection, validation, and collective witnessing for those grieving animal companions. In a culture where pet loss is sometimes dismissed as “lesser,” this experience affirms that love is not measured by species, and grief is not ranked by hierarchy. Michael Bud serves as Creative Producer and Director of Design for Our Loving Companions , shaping the audience experience from arrival through reflection. Working across promotion, staging, production design, and visual storytelling, he translates the project’s artistic and emotional vision into a cohesive immersive environment. His role supports both the creative flow of each performance and the deeper intention to witness, honor, and hold space for those mourning the loss of cherished animal companions. Pamela Hollings (she/they) is a theater-maker, working as a director, dramaturg, educator, actor, deviser and writer, depending on the project. Her career has focused on developing new work; working with playwrights as both director and dramaturg and as a devisor of new work, often site-specific. She is an ensemble member of Aviva Arts (formerly foolsFURY) where most recently they served as a co-writer, dramaturg and performer for Burning Wild a climate catastrophe devised piece performed outdoors in both Sonoma County and San Francisco. She was the Curation & Education Director at 3Girls Theatre, and the Board Chair (2013-2021), as well as an ensemble member (2018-2022) of foolsFURY Theater and the former Artistic Managing Director of both The Yat/Bentley Centre for Performance, SF Bay Area and Soup Kitchen Theatre, Melbourne, Australia. They trained in Theatre Direction at Australia’s National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA) whose distinguished alums include Cate Blanchett, Sara Snook, Baz Luhrmann and many more. Pamela is also a breath practitioner / voice teacher working at the intersection of theatre, education, ritual and somatic wellness. Anna Takayo Walden is a San Francisco-based theatre artist, AEA actor, and the Founding Artistic Director of San Francisco Classical Theatre, a site-specific classical theatre company that launched in June 2026 with a sold-out inaugural reading of Chekhov’s The Seagull directed by Carey Perloff. She is a Directing Fellow at Oakland Theatre Project, a member of the Actors Reading Collective, and Associate Artistic Director of Hawaii Public Theatre. As a director, Anna is drawn to work that lives in the body and in space — theatre that asks audiences not just to watch, but to feel, move, and reckon. Her practice is rooted in classical text, physical theatre, and ensemble, with a particular interest in immersive and site-specific forms that dissolve the boundary between story and world. Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. Her work invites students to explore the foundations of Qigong and Tai Chi as embodied, healing practices that cultivate awareness, vitality, and resilience.

4661d762-c350-5446-80f7-4e7c87973259: 🎧 Deep Listening 🌿 About Event When was the last time you gave yourself the luxury of dedicated listening to an album from beginning to end? Without multitasking, checking your phone, or doing anything else. When was the last time you listened closely to the emotions and desires within you? Deep Listening is an invitation to do both. We’ll gather to listen to Sara Bareilles’ Good Grief in its entirety, setting aside the rare luxury of allowing music to monopolize our attention and wash over us. As we listen together, we’ll also turn our attention inward: to the feelings, memories, questions, and parts of ourselves that the music might bring to the surface. Bring a journal and/or sketchbook as a place for whatever arises to take physical form. You can write, draw, doodle, or simply sit and listen. There’s nothing you need to produce, figure out, or share. Our goal is to simply listen. To notice what’s within us. To give it somewhere to land. To make space for something inside you that may not otherwise get heard. And to do that in the presence of other people, but without any expectation to share or be vulnerable. My own experience has shown me the strength that becomes available to us when we turn inward while surrounded by others who are doing the same. The first part of the gathering is intentionally gentle and private. Afterward, you’ll have the option to stay for a deeper experience of listening, reflection, and sharing in a small group. You don’t need to come with a particular feeling in mind. You don’t need to consider yourself creative. You don’t need to know what you’re looking for. Just bring yourself, something to write or draw with, and a curiosity for what you might discover. 🕰 Flow / Schedule 6:30-7pm · Arrive + Settle In We’ll gather in a circle and begin with gentle movement, think of slow stretches that help us slow down, settle into our bodies, and become present to the experience ahead. 7-7:30pm · Deep Listening We’ll listen to the first portion of Good Grief. Use your journal or sketchbook to write, draw, reflect, or simply listen. 7:30-8pm · Optional Sharing A moment to share anything that surfaced with the wider group. Sharing is always optional. 8-8:30pm · Deeper Listening We’ll listen to the second half of Good Grief. Similar to the first half, use your journal or sketchbook to write, draw, reflect, or simply listen. 8:30-9pm · Small Group Sharing + Closing We’ll split into small groups for facilitated reflection and deeper sharing. 👥 Facilitator Ran Ji created the community version of Deep Listening after experiencing the practice herself several times. Each time, she was surprised by the variety of the emotions, memories, and feelings that surfaced through simply listening to an album with her full attention. She views art as a call and response: an artist puts something deeply personal into the world, and it calls to the parts of us that are ready to hear it. Her hope is to create a space where people can respond to that call with curiosity, privacy, and care. Ran has been a teacher and tutor and has experience facilitating group discussions and helping people open up. More than anything, she brings a deep capacity to sit with people as they are in each moment, without requiring them to explain, perform, or move through their feelings on anyone else's timeline. To learn more about Ran, visit her Instagram. 💫 Who This Is For This space is for anyone who feels called to slow down and listen: to music, to themselves, and to what within might be asking for their attention. WOOD STREET is a feature documentary following members of Oakland’s largest homeless encampment as they fight the city against eviction from their long term community.
