191928a4-6370-564b-9ea6-1429f35d05f3: What if sound is something you felt in the body as much as heard in your ears? Long before it was music, sound served as medicine, prayer, and portal — a technology for shifting consciousness that predates language itself. Join Grammy-nominated artist and teacher Radhika Vekaria for an immersive afternoon built around direct, felt experience: exploring mantra and the intelligence of sound through your own body, breath, and voice. Through direct practice and philosophical insight, this session works with sound as an organizing intelligence, one that refines focus, strengthens presence, and cultivates inner coherence. This is active work: chanting, mudras, and breath practice done together as a group. You will explore: - The relationship between sound and resilience - The deeper meaning behind mantra - Chant as a practice of clarity and courage - Mudra and Nāda yoga as embodied extensions of the practice Rooted in yogic philosophy and grounded in contemporary life, this immersion offers an approach to cultivating steadiness, awareness, and peace. No prior experience is required. The afternoon closes with a 75-minute live performance with Radhika singing in a communal setting, drawing on the same deep lineage that guides the whole workshop. Teacher Bio: Radhika Vekaria is a Grammy®-nominated artist and composer working at the crossing point of Sanskrit and Vedic sacred sound and contemporary music. Her voice draws on devotional and contemporary vocal styles as well as Hindustani classical tradition — she studied for several years under Meher Paralikar, a disciple of Padma Bhushan Pandit Ajoy Chakrabarty of the Patiala-Kasur gharana — alongside classical piano trained since childhood. That grounding shows up in every performance: precise, disciplined, and unmistakably rooted in lineage, even as the music itself moves into new territory. Her project SAPTA: The Seven Ways, an exploration of Vedic mantra, became a healing practice for everyone who encountered it, and made her the first mantra artist to perform at SXSW in 2022. Her 2025 album Warriors of Light earned a Grammy nomination and extended that same inquiry into how ancient sound moves through a contemporary ear. Named after Radha, the Vedic symbol of devotion, she treats sacred sound as a living practice — one she has carried from concert stages to sacred gatherings across the globe. Radhika has performed at Harvard, Omega Institute, the Grammy Museum, and prestigious venues like Estelle Manor and Naviva, reflecting the wide lens through which she is able to convey this wisdom and reach people. Growing up in a British East African Indian family, Radhika was immersed in Vedic rituals since childhood. Learning music from early infancy and with continuous exploration of the multiple arenas of Vedic traditions and philosophy, she has a refreshing approach to how this wisdom can be imbibed and applied in the world today. In 2022, her live audio rooms online reached over 100,000 people with meditation and mantra sessions. She offers a room an experience of return — voice and mantra used deliberately to move people from thinking into feeling, from the head to the heart. That instinct shapes both her performances and her workshops: through similar sessions, she works directly with people's own relationship to sound and voice, drawing on the same tradition and training behind her stage work. For a space built around inquiry and embodied practice, she brings a performance to be moved by, and a practice to be moved through. Explore more at www.radhikavekaria.com

0a96ec18-99af-5dd3-8cd3-473319d81945: Jill McLennan, Walter, 900 years old, watercolor, collage, ink, 26″x20″. photo by artist Jill McLennan’s work gives voice to the harmless, reflecting on the federal government’s decision to rescind the definition of harm (2026) as it applies to the protection of animals and their habitats, listed under the Endangered Species Act (1975). In her art, she depicts animals adapting, inventing new ways to thrive amidst human impact. Using sumi ink, a brush, and mulberry paper, she paints mammals, birds, amphibians, plants, trees, and rivers. Then, tearing the paper, she applies these images to wood panels. Adding watercolor and handmade paper, she creates a transformation from reality to wonder. McLennan states, “The animals are here alongside us, they have always been here, and it is our duty to ensure that they remain, that their habitat is here on earth for generations to come. May my art be a message to harm less, a cry to the present and a hope for the future.” Bio: Jill McLennan creates paintings, collages and prints inspired by her surroundings and the stories that she collects. She has been a member of Mercury 20 Gallery since 2007. She is an active member of her neighborhood, Jingletown Arts, Business + Community (JABC), organizing Open Studios as well as beautification projects. She recently printed a series of linoleum blocks with poems, telling stories of migration and climate change, through a residency at the Kala Art Institute in Berkeley, CA. McLennan has completed two public art projects: Jingletown Birds at 401 Derby and Emeryville Perspectives at 65th and Christie Streets. Both are cut steel fences depicting the local shoreline with birds, designed by McLennan and executed by local metal fabricators. Her work was accepted to the deYoung Open in 2020 and 2023. As an artist and teacher, she is deeply invested in protecting her environment, inspiring the youth, and spreading hope and joy into the world. 16bafeff-ca0c-5b48-a476-5b6576280add: Andrea Brewster, Draft 9, 2026, giclee print, woven vellum. 12″ x 12″, photo courtesy of the artist. Andrea Brewster’s new body of work, Draft, begins with the fundamental structure of weaving: warp and weft, whose interlacing creates both fabric and an underlying grid. She approaches the grid not as a rigid system, but as a living structure capable of variation, interruption, rhythm, and ambiguity. The work draws from weaving drafts, diagrams that function as instructions for generating complex patterns, resembling a form of pre-digital code. The term “draft” also refers to an initial idea or work in progress, connecting structure with imagination and instruction with image.This connection between weaving and digital systems is central to Brewster’s thinking. Although digitally constructed, these pieces retain the appearance of hand-drawn marks, creating a tension between material and virtual, order and improvisation. Through line, color, repetition, and interruption, Brewster explores the relationship between visible patterns and the structures beneath them. Bio: Andrea Brewster is a multidisciplinary artist who investigates the intersection of nature, fiber art, and technology through intricate forms and layered textures. Brewster earned a B.A. in Sculpture from Pomona College and an M.F.A. in New Genres from the San Francisco Art Institute. A 1993 NEA grant recipient, she has exhibited widely in the San Francisco Bay Area, with solo shows at Mercury 20, The Lab, and Southern Exposure, as well as group exhibitions at Metal Haus Gallery, Chandra Cerrito Contemporary, The Oakland Museum, and the Peninsula Museum. Her work has been featured in fiber art exhibitions in Ireland and the U.S. She has participated in the Djerassi Resident Artist Program, and in 2025, her AI work appeared at Load Gallery, Barcelona, and in the book Neo Botanica. She has been a member of Mercury 20 Gallery since 2020. She has obtained exclusive rights to film the fresco through the good graces of Paolo, the museum’s director and her former college sweetheart. Through three time periods and the lives of three couples, THE SECRET MUSEUM explores the mysteries of eros. Lynne Kaufman ( Playwright ) is the author of 20 full-length plays that have been produced in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington D.C., and Louisville at such theatres as Magic Theatre, Actors Theatre of Louisville, TheatreWorks Silicon Valley, and many more –with Shameless Hussy being her most recent work which premiered at The Marsh San Francisco spring 2025. Four of Kaufman’s plays, Extreme Acts, Acid Test, Two Minds , Who Killed Sylvia Plath , and Poetic Justice, have premiered on stage at The Marsh, while two others, Exposing Margaret Mead and The Smartest Woman in America, have appeared on The Marsh’s digital platform MarshStream. Who Killed Sylvia Plath went on to win Best Play in The Marsh’s 2020 MarshStream International Solo Festival. Kaufman’s plays have won many awards including the Glickman Award for Best New Play ( The Couch ), the Kennedy Center’s Fund for New American Plays Award ( Speaking in Tongues ), and the Neil Simon Festival New Play Award ( William Blake in Hollywood ). Kaufman has published four novels, and her short stories have appeared in Cosmopolitan , Redbook , and McCall’s . She was also the recipient of the Otis Guernsey Outstanding New Voice in American Theatre Award from the William Inge Theatre Festival. Warren David Keith ( Director ) is delighted to be reunited with Playwright Lynne Kaufman. His work with her began in 2012 with the Marsh Berkeley premier of Acid Test: The Many Incarnations of Ram Dass , a solo piece in which he played the title role. The play was extended twice in Berkeley then transferred for one performance to a massive tent on Maui, Hawaii where it was seen and enjoyed by Ram Dass and about 300 devoted followers. Subsequently, Acid Test opened at the Marsh San Francisco in 2013 where it also had several runs. Keith has acted in theaters throughout the Bay Area, most recently in 1984 at the Aurora Theatre Company and as the Porter in the California Shakespeare Theater’s production of Macbeth . His film credits include Nomadland , The Last Black Man in San Francisco , Haiku Tunnel , Love and Taxes , Raising Arizona , Fargo , A Serious Man , and The Big Lebowski . As a director he mounted more than 15 productions for American Conservatory Theater’s Young Conservatory Program. He reunited with Ms. Kaufman to direct Who Killed Sylvia Plath and The Smartest Woman in America about the final days of Susan Sontag, both at the Marsh San Francisco. 0772b385-b2b1-44ae-be7d-b3882ec285ad: “One of the most lauded jazz vocalists of her generation” (The New York Times), Tierney Sutton is joined in duo by piano great Tamir Hendelman, exploring the trove of American Songbook classics from her latest album SPRING. Over a career spanning more than three decades, Tierney Sutton has earned international acclaim for her luminous tone, emotional depth, and fearless interpretive artistry. A nine-time GRAMMY nominee, Sutton first rose to prominence through her celebrated work with the Tierney Sutton Band, becoming known for inventive reimaginings of jazz standards and tributes to artists including Joni Mitchell and Frank Sinatra. Her recordings have consistently topped jazz charts while showcasing a rare balance of sophistication and intimacy. Israeli-born pianist Tamir Hendelman is equally revered for his lyrical touch, harmonic brilliance, and dynamic versatility. After moving to Los Angeles as a teenager, Hendelman became a central figure in West Coast jazz, performing with the Clayton-Hamilton Jazz Orchestra, Barbra Streisand, Natalie Cole, and countless leading artists. His elegant playing and sensitive accompaniment have made him one of the most sought-after pianists in contemporary jazz. Together, Sutton and Hendelman share a profound musical chemistry built on nuance, trust, and spontaneity. Their new duo album, SPRING, offers fresh interpretations of beloved standards, transforming familiar melodies into intimate conversations filled with warmth, wit, and timeless beauty. Personnel: Tierney Sutton (vocals); Tamir Hendelman (piano)

8acc4dd7-eadb-4cc3-9de8-6f70c06acf9d: Mothers and Daughters: Writing Formative Relationships in Memoir What does it mean to reckon with the past and find yourself on the other side? In this panel, three She Writes Press memoirists, Robin Rosenbluth, Georgine Hodgkinson, and Rosanne Annoni, explore the profound and complicated ways their mothers shaped them, and the unexpected journeys that led each of them home to herself. From a young white woman navigating the semi-nomadic communities of 1970s Kenya while carrying the wounds of the U.S. foster care system, to a spiritual seeker tracing the long arc between a childhood vision of Christ and a solitary winter at Gampo Abbey, to a college professor who upended her carefully controlled life for the wilds of Puerto Rico's cryptocurrency scene, these are stories of displacement, desire, and hard-won transformation. Moderated by She Writes Press publisher Brooke Warner, this panel is an invitation to explore those moments that break us open and the unlikely places where healing takes root. Each of these memoirs reminds us that growing up isn't something that happens only in childhood, and that our mothers, for better or worse, are the first maps any of us is given to navigate ourselves and our lives. Robin Rosenbluth is a former foster teen who advocates for finding permanent homes for older foster youth. She has worked in the nonprofit sector in New York as a fundraiser, an adjunct professor at Columbia University and New York University. She has studied memoir and the craft of writing with many renowned authors and writes a Substack, My Jagged Journey as a Debut Writer . Robin and her wife have raised two children who now have families of their own. She lives in Brooklyn, New York. Rosanne Annoni was a successful psychotherapist for thirty-five years in the Bay Area before becoming an ordained teacher of the Diamond Approach in 2000. She has taught students and mentored teachers in the United States, the UK, and the EU. In 2024, she was awarded an Emerging Writer Fellowship from Aspen Words. She is married, has one son, and lives with her husband and dog on Cape Cod. Georgine Hodgkinson is a professor of communication studies at Cosumnes River College in Sacramento, where she also served as program coordinator for Re-Emerging Scholars, a program for formerly incarcerated students. Her published scholarship includes book chapters, journal articles, and essays exploring politics, gender, and spirituality. In 2025, she was a People’s Choice Winner for the Amy MacRae International Memoir Award. A certified yoga instructor who loves to run and play pickleball, Georgine splits her time between Dorado, Puerto Rico, and Folsom, California, with her husband, Mark. Brooke Warner is publisher of She Writes Press, a memoir coach, and author of Write On, Sisters!, Green-light Your Book, What's Your Book?, and three books on memoir. She’s a TEDx speaker, weekly podcaster (of “Write-minded” with co-host Grant Faulkner of NaNoWriMo), and publishes a weekly newsletter, Writerly Things, on Substack at brookewarner.substack.com . The narrative follows Mason's journey from the cotton South to metropolitan California, detailing how she crossed the continent, broke free from slavery, and built Black Los Angeles. Through the lens of the Civil War, Reconstruction, and the dawn of Jim Crow, Waite reveals Mason's profound impact on California's history. Los Angeles’s leading Black property owner entered the city as a piece of property herself. Born enslaved in 1818, Biddy Mason was forcibly transported 3,000 miles to California before winning her freedom in a landmark 1856 court case. By the time of her death, she had become one of the wealthiest African Americans in the West – an entrepreneur, philanthropist, and founding mother of Black Los Angeles. The Boundless Biddy Mason: An Odyssey from Slavery to Freedom Across the American West, Kevin Waite’s masterful biography of Mason – the first full-length study of her extraordinary life – places Mason at the center of a larger American story: the expansion of slavery into the West, the legal battles that tested freedom’s meaning, and the rise of a vibrant Black Los Angeles community she helped build. Waite documents Mason’s early years in Mississippi and follows her forced journey across the continent, as one of roughly 1,500 enslaved African Americans who were trafficked from the slave states to the frontier. Her enslaver, Robert Smith, a convert to Mormonism, marched Mason and her children from Mississippi to Utah and ultimately to California. Despite the state’s constitutional ban on slavery, Smith became the largest slaveholder in California, with fourteen people under his control. But it wasn’t until Smith attempted to relocate his human chattel to Texas that the law intervened. A pitched legal battle in Los Angeles resulted in freedom for Mason, her three daughters, and ten other women and children. From that moment forward, Mason reshaped her destiny – and the destiny of her city. She built a respected practice as a nurse and midwife, invested shrewdly in downtown real estate, cultivated influential alliances, and helped found Southern California’s first Black church. Her canny ability to disarm her denigrators with kindness and competence earned Mason a reputation as a leader. Award-winning historian Kevin Waite ably connects Mason’s life to the nation’s great upheavals: the westward expansion of slavery, the Civil War and Reconstruction, and the dawn of Jim Crow. In doing so, he restores Mason to her rightful place in American history, detailing her role as a survivor of forced migration, a litigant in a landmark freedom suit, and an architect of Black Los Angeles. Mason’s legacy in Los Angeles endures to this day, not only as founding member of the First African Methodist Episcopal Church but also in the public works she inspired. “In this astute work of historical recovery, Kevin Waite has provided us with a definitive, modern biography of the remarkable Biddy Mason…a tremendous achievement and a cautionary tale for our own fraught times.” ―Manisha Sinha, author of The Rise and Fall of the Second American Republic: Reconstruction, 1860–1920 “Combining meticulous scholarship with taut, propulsive prose, Kevin Waite tells the story of how the quietly extraordinary Biddy Mason helped break slavery's hold on Southern California. Absorbing and revelatory, this is history at its best.” —Nathaniel Philbrick, National Book Award–winning author of In the Heart of the Sea and The Rush “Kevin Waite has written the book we’ve needed for a long time. Biddy Mason was a most extraordinary woman. With great care and exhaustive research, Kevin Waite has written her biography as part of the stories of enslavement and emancipation as well as faith and community at the western edge of the United States.” —Kelly Lytle Hernández, author of Bad Mexicans Kevin Waite is Anne Stark Watson and Chester Watson Distinguished Professor of History at the University of Texas at Dallas. His first book, West of Slavery , won the 2022 Wiley-Silver Prize and was shortlisted for three other awards, including the Lincoln Prize. His writing appears in The Atlantic , the Los Angeles Times , The Washington Post , Slate , National Geographic , and The New Republic . Kevin moonlights in the TV and film industry, most recently as the writer and producer of a six-episode docuseries on the American Revolution for National Geographic and Disney+. c67e9936-5c4f-511a-a42a-4e413bcd3898: Mark Danner in conversation with Arlie Russell Hochschild · How do we recognize history while we are still living through it? A contested election. A war. A financial collapse. An attack on the Capitol. A democracy transformed. We experience history one event at a time. Only later do we begin to see the connections, and wonder when the world we knew began to change. In Crossing the Rubicon , journalist and political thinker Mark Danner traces twenty-six years of American political life, from the disputed election of 2000 and the War on Terror to the rise and return of Donald Trump, asking how democratic institutions have been tested, weakened, and transformed. Joining him is sociologist Arlie Russell Hochschild , author of Strangers in Their Own Land and Stolen Pride , whose work explores the emotions, identities, and experiences beneath America's political divisions. Together, they bring two extraordinary ways of seeing the same history: the political forces that shape a nation and the human lives shaped by those forces. The evening begins with a short introduction from anthropologist and Clio's founding member Cari Borja , placing the conversation within Clio's larger commitment to the history of ideas, and the importance of gathering to understand the history we are living through. The title reaches back to 49 BCE, when Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon River, setting in motion events that would help bring an end to the Roman Republic. More than two thousand years later, the question remains: How do we know when a society has crossed a threshold from which there may be no return? And what can history teach us about what comes next? Join us for an evening about democracy, power, memory, and the future we are still capable of shaping. Mark Danner has been writing about foreign wars and American politics for more than three decades. Among his books are The Massacre at El Mozote, Torture and Truth, Stripping Bare the Body ,and Spiral: Trapped in the Forever War . He was a staff writer at The New Yorker for many years and is a longtime contributor to The New York Review of Books . His work has received many honors, including a National Magazine Award, three Overseas Press Awards, a Gug- genheim Fellowship, an Emmy, and a MacArthur Fellowship. He is currently Class of 1961 Distinguished Chair in Undergraduate Education at the University of California at Berkeley. Arlie Hochschild ’s latest book is Stolen Pride, Loss, Shame and the Rise of the Right . Now out in paperback with a new Afterword , it was among five non-fiction books Barack Obama selected as favorite books of 2024. It followed Strangers in Their Own Land: Anger and Mourning on the American Right , a National Book Award Finalist and New York Times bestseller. Other of her books include The Second Shift, The Time Bind , and The Managed Heart. Her work has been translated into 18 languages.

Burton is a pioneering expert in complex trauma healing with over 40 years of counseling experience. A nine-time GRAMMY nominee, Sutton first rose to prominence through her celebrated work with the Tierney Sutton Band, becoming known for inventive reimaginings of jazz standards and tributes to artists including Joni Mitchell and Frank Sinatra. Her recordings have consistently topped jazz charts while showcasing a rare balance of sophistication and intimacy. Israeli-born pianist Tamir Hendelman is equally revered for his lyrical touch, harmonic brilliance, and dynamic versatility. After moving to Los Angeles as a teenager, Hendelman became a central figure in West Coast jazz, performing with the Clayton-Hamilton Jazz Orchestra, Barbra Streisand, Natalie Cole, and countless leading artists. His elegant playing and sensitive accompaniment have made him one of the most sought-after pianists in contemporary jazz. Together, Sutton and Hendelman share a profound musical chemistry built on nuance, trust, and spontaneity. Their new duo album, SPRING, offers fresh interpretations of beloved standards, transforming familiar melodies into intimate conversations filled with warmth, wit, and timeless beauty. Personnel: Tierney Sutton (vocals); Tamir Hendelman (piano)

7388a608-497d-5404-8088-18dca87318de: Joshua Jelly-Schapiro in conversation with Nadia Ellis · How does an artist change the way the world sees a place, and ultimately, itself? Harry Belafonte was more than the voice behind “Day-O,” “Jamaica Farewell,” and “Jump in the Line.” The Harlem-born son of Caribbean immigrants brought the music of the islands into American popular culture, becoming a groundbreaking performer whose influence extended far beyond the stage. But behind the music was a life of extraordinary political conviction. From his friendship with Sidney Poitier to his pivotal support of Martin Luther King Jr. and the civil rights movement, Belafonte understood that fame could become a form of power, and that power could be put to work. In Daylight Come: Harry Belafonte and the World He Made , geographer and writer Joshua Jelly-Schapiro explores the remarkable intersections of music, race, migration, celebrity, and political activism, revealing how one artist helped shape both America's imagination of the Caribbean and the course of American history. Joining him is Nadia Ellis , UC Berkeley professor of English and author of Territories of the Soul: Queered Belonging in the Black Diaspora , whose work explores Black diasporic culture, performance, and belonging. The evening begins with an introduction from cultural anthropologist and Clio's founding member Cari Borja , drawing on her doctoral fieldwork in Jamaica to consider how art and performance carry histories, identities, and ideas across borders. Together, they'll explore a question at the heart of Belafonte's life: What happens when an artist becomes not only a voice for a culture, but a force capable of changing the world? An evening about music, memory, Jamaica, the Black diaspora, and the extraordinary possibilities and contradictions, of a life lived in the public eye. Joshua Jelly-Schapiro is a geographer and writer whose books include Daylight Come: Harry Belafonte and the World He Made; Names of New York: Discovering the City’s Past, Present, and Future Through Its Place-Names; and Island People: The Caribbean and the World. He was the co-creator, with Rebecca Solnit, of Nonstop Metropolis: A New York City Atlas, which in 2016 was awarded the Brendan Gill Prize from the Municipal Art Society. His work appears regularly in The New York Review of Books, The New Yorker, and The New York Times, among many other publications, and he is a fellow of the New York Institute for the Humanities. Jelly-Schapiro teaches journalism at New York University and is director of publishing at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn, where he hosts the popular Author Talks series and is coeditor in chief of Pioneer Works Broadcast. Nadia Ellis is a professor in the English Department at UC Berkeley. She's the author of Territories of the Soul: Queered Belonging in the Black Diaspora as well as essays on contemporary Black literature and performance. She is completing a new book about Jamaican religion, ethnography, and aesthetics.

672f901f-a899-4079-b9e5-cf22ee3c1ff5: October Theme: “Broadway and Show Tunes” There’s nothing that brings people together better than singing our favorite songs. It recalls summer nights around the campfire: someone strumming the guitar and all singing a mix of folk music, familiar songs we heard on the radio, and occasional new songs that someone shares. Nobody has to worry about whether you know the songs or can sing like a pro. This is our chance to share the joy of singing simply for the fun of it. Cary Sheldon is a singer, songwriter, and beloved Berkeley voice teacher with 30 years worth of grateful students. She has been playing and teaching in the Bay Area for the last 40 years. Her love for R & B music led her to be part of Zazu Pitts Memorial Orchestra in the 1980’s. Other affiliations include The Henry Kaiser Band, The Henriettas (a recreation of DeZurick sisters, a popular country music duo from the 1940’s), who appeared on Prairie Home Companion, and most recently her band DanceChant, a joyful community-inspired R&B band that encourages audience participation. She continues to be inspired by her love of singing in community. “Singing together with others is one of the greatest joys in my life.” Now in her 60’s, she returns to influences from her early life. Her grade school music teachers included John Langstaff, creator of the Christmas Revels, and the repertoire was based on the American folk tradition, including old English ballads, spirituals, freedom songs, and the popular folk and protest songs of the 1960’s. She hopes to inspire others to explore the depth of this material and rediscover the joy of community singing. Soprano Candace Johnson has led AMN’s Juneteenth Choral Celebration since its inception in 2020. The AMN community knows her through her commitment to the power of the Negro Spirituals tradition, but Candace has a deep connection to theater and to the music of the Broadway stage. A voice instructor at UC Berkeley for 17 years, in 2022 Candace also became the director of the University Gospel Choir. A lyric coloratura soprano, she crosses musical boundaries performing classical, jazz, musical theater, pop and gospel. She has sung on many stages, including Carnegie Hall and The Manhattan Center. Also a playwright and actress, Candace premiered her first one-woman show, Vox in a Box , in UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall in 2018, which led to her becoming a resident solo artist at The Marsh theater (Berkeley/San Francisco). Candace has written and performed 5 full-length one-woman musicals. Her most recent show, Scat-ter Brain: The Music of ADHD , was commissioned by The Marsh in 2024 for its inaugural IFOYE festival of new works by women-identifying playwrights. Following an extended run, Scat-ter Brain was nominated by Broadway World SF for Best Solo Show of 2025. Please read our Health, Safety and COVID-19 Information Our commitment to our patrons

389a2608-8a0a-543f-8d84-ea1abafd4f0a: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.
8010af52-c2d1-5299-b546-ce7d07361509: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.

554453ea-ce41-523c-80ce-5ada220b59ac: 🌿 Description A weekly space for real conversations, meaningful connection, and a deeper sense of belonging. 🌿 About This Gathering Maybe you've got plenty of people in your life, but still sometimes feel lonely. Maybe you find it hard to move beyond small talk and social scripts. Maybe you sometimes struggle to feel like you truly belong, even when you're surrounded by people. Or maybe you're simply curious about what makes some relationships and communities feel easy, genuine, and nourishing — while others don't. Each week, we'll explore a different aspect of connection and belonging: loneliness, vulnerability, authenticity, being seen, boundaries, desire, conflict, and what gets in the way of feeling connected and at home with others. This isn't a workshop where you sit and listen to someone talk about connection. We'll actually practice connecting with one another. You'll have opportunities to share honestly, meet others more deeply, receive support, and explore what's happening in your own relationships and your experience of belonging. ab2bbc13-4594-5e4f-a988-fe404e948cd8: Crisis leadership can be the toughest type of leadership—and the most crucial to master. The aim is to give the body room to express what often has no place in everyday social settings, so the nervous system can process stuck emotion and return toward balance. This session is designed to help you move out of your head and into your body, reset the nervous system toward calm, and support you to reconnect with a more grounded sense of self. ac7c8943-a4d3-400c-b1af-56ef85b73934: Santiago Lastra- Born in Mexico City and raised in Cuernavaca, Santiago Lastra has worked in Michelin-starred establishments around the globe, including the legendary Mugaritz in San Sebastián, Spain and noma in Copenhagen. In October 2020, he opened the doors of KOL in Marylebone, immediately capturing the attention and acclaim of the world’s media. Within three years, KOL secured its first Michelin star, a place on The World’s 50 Best and La Liste, and is regarded as the best Mexican restaurant outside of Mexico. Santiago was also awarded Best Chef at the GQ Food and Drink Awards, and Three Knives by The Best Chef Awards. In 2024, Santiago opened Fonda, a family-style restaurant serving vibrant interpretations of the food found in Mexican markets and homes. Santiago’s ethos is to develop food that celebrates his homeland’s rich cultural tastes, aromas and textures with meticulously sourced seasonal local produce. Mexican Soul is his first book. Mexican Soul - D id you know you can make the best guacamole you’ve ever tasted without using avocado? Or that tortillas and tamales can be made with potato? Through years of research, exploration and cooking in restaurants around the globe, chef Santiago Lastra has discovered a secret: you can make incredible Mexican food without having to hunt down specific ingredients or buy traditional produce that has lost its freshness by the time it lands in your kitchen. Mexican flavor can be unlocked anywhere in the world, with almost any ingredient, and this book is the key to finding it. By breaking down the basics of Mexican flavour profiles then exploring how you can find a wide variety of these elements in your home kitchen, Santiago shows a new way of understanding one of the richest cuisines on the planet so that anything from a Salsa Macha and Tomato and Cherry Aguachile to Tinga Tostadas and Chocolate Tamales with Chocolate and Mezcal Cream can be on the table in minutes, regardless of what you have to hand. Get ready to discover Mexican Soul: A New Style of Cooking .
bb52dcc6-a1c9-5c02-a86f-e44ae11ece17: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

3d0c53c1-23fe-51f1-813c-5d4d256529a5: What would make you believe the impossible? · What happens when the desire to know becomes inseparable from the desire for something to be true? We like to imagine reason as solid ground, but grief, love, memory, and loss can make the boundaries between evidence, belief, obsession, and hope much harder to see. In their debut novels, Scott Lambridis and Yance Wyatt explore characters confronting realities that strain the explanations available to them. Their conversation will move between psychology, science, faith, mythology, and the impossible to ask what makes a belief reasonable, where skepticism becomes its own kind of certainty, and whether emotion distorts inquiry or gives it urgency. At stake is a deeply human question: when ordinary explanations fail us, what are we willing to believe in order to keep making sense of the world? Scott Lambridis writes literary speculative fiction about the stories people rely on to make sense of the world. He studied neurobiology before earning an MFA in Fiction from San Francisco State University. His fiction explores belief, consciousness, trauma, and the strange places where psychology, folklore, and love begin to overlap. Before publishing his debut novel, St. Ulphia’s Dead, Scott toured with a progressive rock band, founded an independent press and literary performance series, tended a forty-acre olive farm, and read a book from every country in the world. He lives in Bellingham, Washington, with his family. More at scottlambridis.com . Yance Wyatt was born and raised in Nashville, Tennessee. He studied fiction at the University of Cambridge and the University of Southern California, where he has gone on to serve as professor of writing and director of the Writing Center. As fiction editor with The Blue Mountain Review, he seeks to acquire the best new stories from the South. His own stories have appeared in dozens of nationally circulated literary journals and received several Pushcart Prize nominations. The Watersmith is his first novel. Visit him @yancewyatt or www.yancewyatt.com .

4062dd46-ca7d-47af-b089-284e2b45f3fd: One of today’s premier jazz drummers · "The Groove Master", Herlin Riley is widely considered one of the best drummers in any genre of music performing today. The longtime drummer for the legendary Ahmad Jamal and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra now leads two groups, his quintet and the New Orleans Groove Masters featuring himself, Jason Marsalis, and Shannon Powell. Herlin’s most recent album, Perpetual Optimism, reunites the quintet of rising stars that Riley assembled for his Mack Avenue Records debut, New Direction. Since the release of that acclaimed album, all four of Riley’s bandmates – trumpeter Bruce Harris, saxophonist Godwin Louis, pianist Emmet Cohen, and bassist Russell Hall – have been making major waves across the modern jazz scene, attesting to the master drummer’s Art Blakey-like ear for talent and sage musical guidance. Herlin Riley's source of strength comes from his faith in God, his wife of four decades, and his family of five children and 10 grandchildren; his lifelong home in New Orleans, the creative community that surrounds it, and his positive approach to life and music. His roots in the church are also vital, shining through in the congregational claps that help establish the celebratory spirit that is showcased in the album opener “Rush Hour.” He also relies on his musical family, including his long-established ties with Wynton Marsalis and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra. Riley’s connection to the Marsalis dynasty traces back a generation earlier, to family patriarch and fellow lifelong New Orleanian Ellis Marsalis. It was while performing with Ellis at the annual New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival in a trio with bassist Reginald Veal that Riley first caught the ear of Wynton, who invited both members of his father’s rhythm section to join him, launching a vital relationship that’s now lasted more than three decades. Riley pays homage to his mentor on the closing track of Perpetual Optimism, the funky arrangement of Ellis Marsalis’ composition “Twelve’s It.” In the quintet’s lively rendition, the tune is not just a cover but a tribute, as Riley intones a short ode to passing the torch that refers to the elder Marsalis as “a great musician who taught a whole lot of fellows.” Another Crescent City icon, the late singer, pianist, songwriter, and producer Allen Toussaint, was the motivator behind Riley’s other vocal turn on the album, a gritty take on Willie Dixon’s blues classic “Wang Dang Doodle.” Toussaint stopped in to hear Riley play at a New Orleans club and heard the drummer’s 5/4 arrangement of the familiar standard. “He was really impressed,” Riley recalls. “He said, ‘Wow, man, I’ve heard ‘Wang Dang Doodle’ a thousand times, but I’ve never heard it performed in 5 before. You should record that.’ A few months later, he passed away, so I recorded the tune to pay homage to the wishes of the great Allen Toussaint.” Though he conveys vivid emotion in his voice, Riley stops short of calling himself a singer. His willingness to step to the mic comes from advice he was given by New Orleans vocal great Germaine Bazzle. “She’s a very elegant and regal lady, but when she’s performing, she scats, rolls her shoulders, dances, and really engages in the music with honesty and passion,” says Riley. When he asked her how she reconciled those two extremes, Bazzle told him, “’ You have to allow yourself to become emotionally naked when you’re on the bandstand.’ When she said that, a light bulb went off in my head. I’m not a singer, but I just do what I do, and I have the audacity to be uninhibited.” The same can be said for Riley’s work behind the kit, where he leads his stellar band with infectious enthusiasm and bristling swing. His “Be There When I Get There” captures the anticipation and excitement of rushing to an eagerly awaited appointment, whether a romantic rendezvous, a gathering of friends, or a night of music. The brisk “Borders Without Lines” comes from the pen of Riley’s Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra bandmate Victor Goines, while the classic “You Don’t Know What Love Is” becomes a sultry simmer, highlighted by Harris’ mournful, muted trumpet. The title track is the rare Riley original composed in a major key, and its sunny disposition perfectly communicates his unflagging hopefulness. The lovely “Touched,” featuring Louis’ achingly lyrical alto, recalls a tender moment with the drummer’s mother before she passed away. “I was in her room in her last days, and she rubbed my head. I’m a grown man, but I felt like an innocent child. There’s a special love wrapped in the touch of a mother of every living creature. That special euphoria only comes from her.” The bittersweet “Wings and Roots” looks to the next generation, referring to Riley’s philosophy of raising children: “You have to root them in good values and fundamental characteristics, but once they get to be a certain age, you have to give them the wings to be free, to go out and be themselves.” Finally, “Stella By Starlight” is another nod to the American Songbook, taken at a graceful midtempo pace with Cohen’s deft touch over Riley’s sensitive brushwork. In the end, Riley hopes that the music of Perpetual Optimism helps spread the upbeat manifesto that he’s chosen to live by. “I always look forward, no matter what happens in life. If you’re grieving or faced with an emotional challenge, keep in mind: If you’re still breathing, there’s a chance that you can overcome and thrive. Commit yourself to PERPETUAL OPTIMISM!”

608286a7-eee3-5de4-a1cb-373ee4cf70d5: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com

3987f64f-0b81-4532-a1f3-a44a9f3cd912: An inspiring guide that reimagines the stages of grief into five healing actions, Reimagining Grief offers light and a new way forward in the midst of darkness. This is the book Kate wishes she'd had, and she wrote it for you. Kate will be joined in conversation by Myra Sacks, the author of award-winning memoir, " Fifty-Seven Fridays: Losing Our Daughter Finding Our Way ," and founder of E-Motion, Inc. There is no way to spin grief. It's hard. It's messy. It's destabilizing. And every single one of us has to go through it. Author and grief coach Kate Doerge knows this too well. Over six years, she lost her father to heart failure and her mother in a car accident five days before Christmas. She also faced the hardest challenge for any parent, losing her sixteen-year-old daughter, Penny, to complications from a rare genetic condition. After Penny's death, Kate knew she had a choice, she could lose herself to a grief so powerful she might not come back from it—or she could find another way through. Reimagining Grief is the result of that search. Drawing from her own experience, the latest research, and conversations with others who have faced devastating loss, Kate offers five actions that can help ground you when you feel out of control, lift you when you're depleted, and help you process the pain of loss. In this book, you'll learn: Why There Isn’t One Right Way to Grieve — and How to Find Your Own Path An Approach to Saying Goodbye That Honors Both You and Your Loved One The 5 Actions Through Grief — and How to Use Them to Heal What Post-Traumatic Growth Really Looks Like How to Find Joy Again Turning Pain into Purpose These actions won’t make grief vanish or disappear; everyone has to go through the difficult path that you are put on after losing someone you loved deeply. However, Reimagining Grief offers some light and healing in the midst of darkness and a different way forward. This is the book Kate wishes she'd had. She wrote it for you. Kate Doerge is a USA TODAY bestselling author, motivational speaker, certified grief coach, and founder of Penny’s Flight Foundation. Through heartfelt storytelling, research-backed insights, and practical strategies, Kate inspires audiences to navigate change, embrace resilience, and lead lives filled with greater purpose and connection. Myra Sack is the author of award-winning memoir, " Fifty-Seven Fridays: Losing Our Daughter Finding Our Way ," and founder of E-Motion, Inc. a nonprofit organization created to support community, movement and ritual to enhance coping and resilience. Myra's life changed when her older daughter, Havi, died in January 2021. Blending Myra's lived experience and knowledge as a certified Compassionate Bereavement Care provider with her lifelong identity as an athlete and career in social impact, E-Motion evolved out of a new way of living with the most difficult reality. Myra holds an MBA in Social Impact from Boston University, and graduated with a B.A. cum laude from Dartmouth College, where she captained the women's soccer team and earned All-America honors. Myra serves on the Board of the Courageous Parents Network. adf26ce2-c44b-4c7a-a37e-010d2aa33aa4: Matt shares his dramatic tale of gentlemen-explorers of the 1930s racing to find and harvest a poisonous Amazon vine. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Thursday, November 12 at 7:00 PM when Matt O'Hara comes to the store to present his new book The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon . Matt will be joined by Rebecca Herman for the conversation and will sign copies of his book after the presentation. In the fall of 1938, a young, frail American explorer set off down a river in the western Amazon in search of curare, a poison he thought might save his life. Richard Gill had learned that local tribes used curare-laced blow darts to kill animals, but it was also potentially a cure for many ailments, including his own. He also thought he could make a fortune by connecting the knowledge of two worlds. Obsessed with curare, he raced to make deals with Indigenous poison masters in the Amazon and pharmaceutical companies back home, even as his Russian-born rival Boris Krukoff sought to do the same. In The Flying Death , the historian Matt O'Hara asks who and what we are willing to sacrifice in the name of discovery and profit. O'Hara brings to life Gill's epic quest, a stranger-than-fiction true story that moves from unexplored territory in the Amazon to rogue medical trials and cutthroat corporate boardrooms in the United States. Navigating treacherous terrain and politics, Gill and Krukoff successfully created a veritable curare–industrial complex, as the plant became a key element in shock therapy, transformed surgery in the United States and across the globe, and eventually led to a Nobel Prize. The Flying Death offers a thrilling ride across Indigenous knowledge, scientific exploration, and exploitation, unearthing a story of discovery that poses searching questions about the price of progress, who pays it, and who gets credit. MATT O'HARA is a professor of history at the University of California, Santa Cruz. He is the award-winning author of many journal articles and two books, The History of the Future in Colonial Mexico and A Flock Divided: Race, Religion, and Politics in Mexico, 1749–1857. REBECCA HERMAN is Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley, where she teaches about environmental politics, US-Latin American relations, and modern Latin America. 06b8ff04-ab15-4e66-a82c-89c13ed77627: Contemporary saxophonist, author, and music producer Jackiem Joyner is set to release his 7th album, Touch, worldwide this fall, 2019. After more than 12 years as a recording artist, Jackiem continues to stand out with electrifying live performances and brilliant music productions. As a performer, he has toured over 30 countries and performed with the likes of the late George Duke, Marcus Miller, Keiko Matsui, Donnie McClurkin, Angela Bofill, Najee, Kirk Whalum, Peter White, and many, many more. Joyner’s radio success is widely known within the industry. Joyner has two number-one hit songs, five top 10 Billboard singles, and a number-one debut album under his belt. In addition, he published the highly acclaimed science fiction novel Zarya , which received high praise and a five-star rating on Amazon. “This album is about romance,” Joyner explains of Touch . “I wanted to give everyone something hip, smooth, and sexy at the same time.” The record has an urban feel, laced with the hottest downtempo vibes. The album shares similar textures to the music of artists Tank and Trey Songz. Joyner’s soprano sax leads the charge through most of the album. “My approach to performing on this record was to be melodic and dynamic with my horn”. Peter White joins Jackiem on the first single, “Last Dance”. The combination of soprano sax and nylon guitar pulls you in with its romantic and catchy melody. Najee serves up the flute on a dreamy urban song called “Fairytales”. The unique mix of flute and soprano sax on this vibey tune forms one of Joyner’s best performances and productions. The song was written together with Tim Bailey, aka Twizzboy. Born to a Vietnam War veteran father and a dedicated mother in Norfolk, VA, growing up wasn’t easy for Jackiem. He set his sights high from a young age; he always dreamed of being a performing artist, as unlikely as it was, given his humble upbringing. Even as a child, he loved the attention he received from his family when he danced to Michael Jackson songs. Now, Jackiem is proud to stand front and center on the main stage most weekends around the country. A quick glance at Joyner’s track record makes it clear that he continues to beat the odds in a tough and competitive music industry. “I love what I do, and I have passion”, Jackiem says. “I don’t care how hard things get, it’ll never stop me from doing what I love: playing the sax, writing music and stories, and performing live.” His love of writing novels came as a surprise to many of his fans. “I’m very excited to release my second novel soon after my album release,” Joyner says. “Writing stories is now a big part of my creative journey.” The first single from Joyner’s last album, Main Street Beat (2017), was named for his daughter, Trinity. Joyner’s adoration for his little girl is clearly expressed through the live, pop-influenced song, driven by Steve Oliver’s guitar. The song was an instant hit. Reaching no. 2 on the Billboard. We’re all dying to see if she follows in dad’s footsteps with her own stage career someday! With the creation of his company, JOYNER MEDIA COMPANY L.L.C., Joyner hopes to inspire other creators to follow their dreams and realize their true potential in art and multimedia. When Jackiem is not touring the world, he spends time giving lectures to students across the country. He also enjoys talking to band classes, helping them with practice, and offering insight on how to pursue a career in the performing arts. Currently, Joyner is on a US tour in support of his new album, Touch . He will be touring Los Angeles, CA – Washington, DC – Hampton, VA – Melbourne, FL – Detroit, MI – Chicago, IL – Charleston, SC – Houston, TX – Rehoboth Beach, DE – Mazlatan, Mexico – Syracuse, NY – Tampa, FL – Atlanta, GA, and many more cities.

540d7871-e687-4aab-aa9f-d474db637e81: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: School Fair School Fair (Findlay Buchanan, Semisi Ma’ia’i, Hamish Morgan, De Stevens and Rose Pickernell) make music embedded in the human experience. It’s a product of the band’s native New Zealand, a place that remains intimate and remote, where emotion is magnified over both distance and familiarity. The five band members began the project renting out a factory-sized, sub-zero degree Celsius room normally operated by construction workers in the industrial area of Ōtepoti, Dunedin, New Zealand in 2021, recording music on the 4-track tape recorder that would become debut Gorse on a Hill . The album remained the only trace of the band online for a few years, an artifact for those who know where to look. School Fair’s music has this sense of self-discovery when you find it, a sound that feels both recognizable and like the vacant expanse of a country whirring by on a train. Still with little to no self-promotion, the appearance of sophomore effort Bird the Kid online in early 2025 was a new portal to their world of melodic and intricate indie music that retains a kind of atmospheric beauty. Unexpected Violence (Mutual, 2026) is the first record made between geographical places, with the band now split in between London and New Zealand. You can hear this fragmented approach in the patchwork quality and inherent connective tissue of the album. Recorded initially in a studio in East London, it was the first time the band brought in an outside engineer (Syd Kemp?), as opposed to the band’s prior live recordings, where the tendency was to “feed back off each other in quite a messy abstract and complicated way that works for us but isn’t typically structured.” The band then took these recordings and evolved them back home in Dunedin, with the addition of vocals on some tracks by Pickernell adding to the cohesive energy and collective, dialed-in synergy of the quintet. School Fair is built upon the many eclectic mediums from which the band members individually create: time spent repairing old machines, making short films, metalworking and jewelry-making, writing and engineering. All these counterparts bring a kind of industrial electricity to the music where each part feels necessary and agile, as well as perfectly in conjunction. It’s these points beneath the surface where the songs really bloom. The moody transference of guitar lick to guttural vocal and back again, where melody conjoins with surprising inflection and sharp-hued ambiance, littered with both poetic spoken-word and a self-referentiality of clues and repetition that rewards close listening yet remains accessible and immediate. Transportive lyrics shine with the lore and mythology of a world that is both deeply specific and transcendent in its curiosity toward the surrounding environment. Unexpected Violence is filled with resounding descriptors: from “cat runs blind in the smoke / birds slap their wings away / trees thrash and crash / each lonely in their chosen way” (the meandering “Angelika”) or the consequently spellbinding phrasing of “come out to your dead animal river gushing hard / come out to your heart split open and lit up with stars” of “In Boredom You Shoot Your Gun”. It’s a starkly poetic snapshot into the band’s own universe and a showcase in the thoroughfare of language, where the specificity of one person’s memory counteracts with a landscape that blurs and unravels with the passage of time. Unexpected Violence a record that could only be made in a place like New Zealand, yet its vantage point expands far beyond to the vast unwieldiness of human sentiment. “There’s a sense of remoteness to the record, both emotionally but also in the sense of place, broken farms, cast iron beaches, blank midday fires, lost friends.” Or as the band recites in the austere glimmer of “Spirally Staircase Memory”: “memories are just stories that can’t be found.” But School Fair reaches some sort of access point, a way for them to live on. The name Unexpected Violence was born out of Buchanan and Ma’ia’i coming across the genre title in a bookstore in Berlin, and is a fitting discernment of the heartbreak that often comes with the realities of existence. In album highlight “Gussied Up,” the band intones: “I never never never ever / wanna hear you / see you, feel you or touch you.” It’s a harsh statement that feels swept up in the parallel admission that these are relationships you may never fully escape; they have left their mark. We still pass the places they inhabit, and feel the uncanny emptiness even after moving on. It’s fitting that the record ends on a similar contradiction. Just discernable above spirals of drummed up, ambient noise: “I miss you now you’re gone.” For all things can be true at once. Between them, 2022 NEA Jazz Master Stanley Clarke and 1998 NEA Jazz Master Ron Carter have defined and redefined the bass’s role in modern jazz, from the hard bop innovations of the early 1960s to the jazz-fusion revolution of the 1970s and 1980s. The four-time GRAMMY winning Clarke achieved worldwide fame as a pioneer of jazz fusion with Chick Corea and Return to Forever, and his subsequent career as a bandleader. The Philadelphia native has recorded 24 albums as a leader, leading a procession of masterful bands, and collaborating with George Duke, McCoy Tyner, Dexter Gordon, Freddie Hubbard, Al Di Meola, Paul McCartney, Keith Richards, Stewart Copeland, and dozens more. Ron Carter is, quite simply, the face of jazz bass. A towering figure, he was already a creative force on the roiling early ‘60s scene when he joined Miles Davis in 1962, the first piece of what became the trumpeter’s second great quintet. With more than 2,300 albums to his credit, including over 60 as a leader, "The Maestro” holds the Guinness World Record as jazz’s most recorded bassist. Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. Her work invites students to explore the foundations of Qigong and Tai Chi as embodied, healing practices that cultivate awareness, vitality, and resilience.

An ensemble cast collides and crosses paths in their small corner of the Midwest where no one is a stranger: the baker, the realtor, the poet, the gardener, the frustrated artist. In Devon Halliday’s transcendent debut novel, secrets turn contagious, impulses transform into resolutions, and no one is certain whether they will remain in the confines of their Appalachian college town or step out into the unknown. Surrounded by hills, buried in green, Eden is a forgotten town full of ordinary lives. But over the course of a humid summer week, seven of these ordinary lives reach their boiling point, as the existential questions of each begin to urgently entwine. Underneath the threat of marital infidelity, financial ruin, and life-changing illness is always the same question: To stay, or to go? If you choose to stay, is it ever a permanent choice? Can you be sure you’ll choose it again tomorrow? A mosaic portrait of love and its close substitutes, the novel suggests, fearfully, that even our best decisions might be fragile, arbitrary, and impermanent. “This brims with insights into the human condition.”— Publishers Weekly “A heartfelt debut … Halliday offers varied, honest looks at the intimate struggles that accompany life’s unexpected turning points.”— Booklist “Devon Halliday has such a mastery of language and storytelling artistry that it’s hard to believe To Stay, To Stay, To Stay is her debut. This novel, a wry and incisive exploration of how people behave (and misbehave) at the critical inflection points in their lives, is a marvel.”—Marisa Silver, author of At Last “In this enchanting tale of small-town love, artisanal bread, and sketchy real estate, Devon Halliday explores the webs that connect us and the mysterious forces that break those webs apart. Everything and everyone in this wonderful novel is rendered with precision, wit, and uncompromising humanity.”—David Haynes, author of Martha’s Daughter “With rare emotional precision and a fierce, glowing heart, Devon Halliday investigates the stories people tell themselves about love and the combustible, constant anxieties that sustain those stories. This marvelous debut novel wisely asks an urgent, contemporary question: What’s braver? Blowing up your life? Or simply living it, however it unfolds?”—Dean Bakopoulos, author of Summerlong “What a delightful debut novel by Devon Halliday—its pages full of sun and shadow, love and gravity. To Stay, To Stay, To Stay handles its cast of characters with deftness and grace, showing us the many facets of people in a small town as they connect and disconnect from one another.”—Alix Ohlin, author of Dual Citizens “A preternaturally wise and wickedly ambitious debut. Halliday’s small town and big cast of characters cast a spell under which I would happily have stayed, stayed, stayed. Alas, the ending is perfection, too.”—Anna Solomon, author of The Book of V Devon Halliday is a Pushcart Prize winner and a Rona Jaffe Foundation Graduate Fellow.
